prompt: Which connector is now the universal standard on modern Android phones, laptops, and tablets for both data and charging, and is reversible so it works in either orientation?

options.text: Lightning
Micro-USB
USB-C
Mini-USB

explanation: USB-C (Type-C) is reversible, supports USB 3.x speeds, Thunderbolt 4, DisplayPort Alt Mode, and USB Power Delivery up to 240W. It is universal across modern Android phones, iPads, MacBooks, and most laptops. Lightning was Apple's proprietary connector for older iPhones — replaced by USB-C starting with iPhone 15. Micro-USB was the previous Android standard — slower and directional (only one way). Mini-USB is an older standard seen on cameras and older external drives. For 220-1201: know all connector types and which devices use them.

prompt: A laptop advertises 178-degree viewing angles and accurate color reproduction suitable for photo editing. Which panel technology does it MOST likely use?

options.text: TN (Twisted Nematic)
IPS (In-Plane Switching)
CRT
Plasma

explanation: IPS (In-Plane Switching) panels offer consistent, accurate color from virtually any angle (178° horizontal and vertical) and are the standard for professional photo/video work and quality laptops. Trade-off: slightly slower pixel response than TN panels. TN panels: fastest response (1ms), best for competitive gaming — terrible viewing angles and color accuracy. OLED: self-emitting pixels, perfect blacks, infinite contrast — premium phones and high-end laptops. VA: better contrast than IPS, better angles than TN — common in budget monitors. For 220-1201: know all four panel types and their trade-offs.

prompt: A tablet screen displays a perfect image but does not respond to any touch input at all. Which component has MOST likely failed?

options.text: LCD backlight
GPU
Digitizer
Battery

explanation: The digitizer is the transparent capacitive touch-sensing layer on top of the display panel. It detects touch and converts it to digital coordinates — completely separate from the display itself. When the digitizer fails, the screen still shows images normally (the LCD or OLED panel is fine) but touch input stops entirely. A failed backlight causes a dim or black screen. On modern devices the digitizer is often fused to the glass — a cracked digitizer usually means replacing the full display assembly. The key diagnostic: image is fine but touch is dead = digitizer. Image is dark or absent = backlight, GPU, or cable.

prompt: Which short-range wireless technology enables contactless payments like Apple Pay and Google Pay by bringing a device within about 4 centimeters of a terminal?

options.text: Bluetooth 5.0
NFC
Wi-Fi Direct
RFID (125 kHz)

explanation: NFC (Near Field Communication) operates at 13.56 MHz with a range under 4 cm, making accidental eavesdropping extremely difficult. Uses: contactless payments (Apple Pay, Google Pay), transit card taps, Bluetooth quick-pair, and small data transfers. The very short range is a security feature. Bluetooth 5.0: up to 400 m (Class 1) — used for peripherals, headphones, speakers. Wi-Fi Direct: peer-to-peer Wi-Fi without an access point — used for screen mirroring and file transfer. RFID at 125 kHz: one-way, read-only, used in older access badges and inventory tags. NFC is bidirectional — both devices can send and receive.

prompt: A user achieves multi-gigabit download speeds on 5G in a downtown area but loses signal when entering buildings. Which 5G frequency band is providing these speeds?

options.text: Low-band 5G (sub-1 GHz)
Mid-band 5G (C-band, 2.5–6 GHz)
mmWave 5G (24–100 GHz)
4G LTE-A

explanation: mmWave (millimeter wave) 5G operates at 24–100 GHz and delivers multi-gigabit speeds (2–10 Gbps) with extremely low latency. Drawbacks: very poor building penetration and limited range (hundreds of meters) — requires dense small cell deployment in urban cores. Low-band 5G: excellent nationwide coverage and building penetration, speeds similar to fast 4G LTE (100–300 Mbps). Mid-band 5G (C-band): the best balance — good speed (500 Mbps–2 Gbps) with reasonable coverage and some building penetration. Most carrier deployments focus on C-band for the best user experience. The 220-1201 exam tests all three 5G band characteristics.

prompt: A technician is upgrading RAM in a laptop. Which RAM form factor is standard for laptops?

options.text: SO-DIMM
UDIMM
RDIMM
LRDIMM

explanation: SO-DIMM (Small Outline DIMM) is the laptop form factor — physically smaller than desktop DIMMs. DDR4 SO-DIMM: 260 pins. DDR5 SO-DIMM: 262 pins. Desktop DDR4 DIMM: 288 pins. Many modern ultrabooks and MacBooks use soldered LPDDR5/5X — permanently attached to the motherboard and not user-upgradeable. Always check before purchasing: is the laptop's RAM socketed (SO-DIMM) or soldered? UDIMM: standard unbuffered desktop memory. RDIMM: registered server memory for large-capacity configurations. LRDIMM: load-reduced server memory. For 220-1201: laptop = SO-DIMM or soldered; desktop = DIMM.

prompt: A company issues smartphones to employees and needs to enforce PIN requirements, restrict camera use, and remotely wipe devices if stolen. Which technology enables this?

options.text: NFC device management
MDM — Mobile Device Management
Bluetooth tethering policy
GPS tracking only

explanation: MDM (Mobile Device Management) platforms (Microsoft Intune, Jamf, VMware Workspace ONE) allow IT to: enforce passcode complexity, disable hardware features (camera, microphone, USB), push and remove apps remotely, enforce encryption, locate devices via GPS, remotely lock, and perform remote wipe. Devices must be MDM enrolled — either by the user (BYOD/self-enrollment) or pre-enrolled by IT (corporate). MDM can containerize work apps separately from personal apps on BYOD devices, allowing corporate data wipe without touching personal data. Without MDM, there is no centralized way to enforce policies or remotely wipe a lost device.

prompt: Which mobile feature allows a smartphone to share its cellular data connection with a laptop or other device wirelessly?

options.text: NFC pairing
Bluetooth audio
Personal hotspot / tethering
AirDrop

explanation: Personal hotspot (iOS) or Mobile Hotspot (Android) allows a smartphone to act as a portable Wi-Fi router, sharing its cellular data connection with up to several other devices wirelessly. USB tethering shares the connection via USB cable — faster and charges the phone simultaneously. Bluetooth tethering: shares data via Bluetooth — slower than Wi-Fi hotspot. Carrier plans may restrict or charge extra for hotspot use. AirDrop: Apple-proprietary file sharing between Apple devices via Bluetooth + Wi-Fi Direct — NOT for sharing internet. NFC pairing: establishes Bluetooth or Wi-Fi connections quickly — not an internet sharing technology.

prompt: Which cable category supports 10 Gbps Ethernet at the full 100-meter distance and is the current standard for new commercial installations?

options.text: Cat5e
Cat6
Cat6a
Cat3

explanation: Cat6a (Augmented Cat6) supports 10GBASE-T at the full 100-meter segment length. The 'augmented' spec reduces alien crosstalk compared to standard Cat6. Cat5e: 1 Gbps at 100 m (common in older buildings). Cat6: 10 Gbps only up to 55 m; drops to 1 Gbps at 100 m. Cat6a: 10 Gbps at full 100 m — recommended for new installations. Cat8: 25/40 Gbps but only 30 m — data center use only (server-to-switch connections). Fiber optic: multi-mode up to ~550 m (OM4), single-mode up to tens of kilometers — immune to EMI. All copper Ethernet uses the 100 m segment rule except Cat8 (30 m).

prompt: Which protocol automatically provides IP addresses, subnet masks, default gateways, and DNS server addresses to client devices on a network?

options.text: DNS
DHCP
ARP
SNMP

explanation: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) uses ports 67 (server) and 68 (client) over UDP. The DORA process: Discover (client broadcasts), Offer (server proposes IP), Request (client accepts), Acknowledge (server confirms). If DHCP fails, Windows self-assigns an APIPA address (169.254.x.x). DNS (port 53): resolves hostnames to IP addresses. ARP: resolves IP addresses to MAC addresses on the local segment. SNMP (161/162): monitors and manages network devices. DHCP leases are temporary — clients renew at 50% of lease time. Static IPs bypass DHCP and are used for servers, printers, and network devices needing consistent addresses.

prompt: A user cannot access any websites by name but can access them by IP address. Which service has MOST likely failed?

options.text: DHCP
DNS
HTTP
FTP

explanation: DNS (Domain Name System, port 53) resolves hostnames (like google.com) to IP addresses. If DNS fails, hostnames cannot be resolved — but direct IP access still works because no name resolution is needed. Confirming DNS failure: ping google.com fails but ping 8.8.8.8 succeeds. Fix: check DNS server setting in ipconfig /all, try setting DNS manually to 8.8.8.8 (Google) or 1.1.1.1 (Cloudflare), run ipconfig /flushdns to clear stale cache entries. DHCP failure causes APIPA (169.254.x.x) — no IP at all, not just DNS. HTTP failure means web server is down — the issue would be specific to that site, not all sites.

prompt: Which Wi-Fi standard introduced Multi-Link Operation (MLO), allowing devices to transmit across multiple frequency bands simultaneously, and carries the Wi-Fi 7 designation?
explanation: 802.11be (Wi-Fi 7): introduced Multi-Link Operation (MLO) — a device can simultaneously use multiple bands (2.4/5/6 GHz) for aggregated throughput and reduced latency. Theoretical max: 46 Gbps. Wi-Fi generation quick reference: 802.11b = Wi-Fi 1 (11 Mbps), 802.11a/g = Wi-Fi 2/3 (54 Mbps), 802.11n = Wi-Fi 4 (600 Mbps, dual-band), 802.11ac = Wi-Fi 5 (3.5 Gbps, 5 GHz), 802.11ax = Wi-Fi 6 (9.6 Gbps, OFDMA), 802.11ax + 6 GHz = Wi-Fi 6E, 802.11be = Wi-Fi 7 (46 Gbps, MLO). The 220-1201 adds Wi-Fi 7 as a tested standard.

prompt: A network administrator needs to power IP cameras requiring 25W each over Cat6a cable with no separate power outlet available. Which PoE standard is the MINIMUM that meets this requirement?

options.text: 802.3bt Type 3 (PoE++) — 60W
Standard Ethernet — no power

explanation: PoE standards and power budgets: 802.3af (PoE): 15.4W per port max — VoIP phones, basic APs, low-power cameras. 802.3at (PoE+): 30W per port max — most IP cameras, mid-range APs, PTZ cameras. 802.3bt Type 3 (PoE++): 60W — high-end APs, video conferencing systems. 802.3bt Type 4: 100W — thin clients, LED panels. At 25W the camera exceeds PoE's 15.4W but fits within PoE+'s 30W budget. Both switch port and device must support the same PoE standard. PoE injectors add PoE to individual ports on non-PoE switches — useful for adding a single camera without replacing the entire switch.

prompt: Which network device forwards frames based on MAC addresses, creates a separate collision domain for each port, and operates at OSI Layer 2?

options.text: Hub
Router
Switch
Modem

explanation: A managed or unmanaged switch operates at Layer 2 (Data Link) and learns MAC addresses dynamically to build a forwarding table. It sends frames only to the correct destination port — unlike a hub which broadcasts to all ports. Each switch port is its own collision domain, eliminating collisions entirely. All switch ports share one broadcast domain (unless VLANs are configured). Hub: Layer 1 — shares bandwidth among all ports, all in one collision domain, obsolete. Router: Layer 3 — routes between different IP networks using IP addresses. Modem: converts analog signals (coax, phone line, fiber) to digital Ethernet — connects the home/office to the ISP.

prompt: A workstation with IP 192.168.10.50/24, gateway 192.168.10.1, can ping the gateway but cannot browse any websites. Pinging 8.8.8.8 by IP succeeds. What is the problem?

options.text: The subnet mask is incorrect
The default gateway is misconfigured
DNS is not configured or not reachable
The workstation's NIC is failing

explanation: The test results tell the full story: pinging the gateway (192.168.10.1) confirms the physical connection and local routing work correctly. Pinging 8.8.8.8 (an internet IP) confirms the path to the internet works — packets are reaching external servers. Failing to browse websites by name means hostname-to-IP resolution (DNS) is broken. Without a functioning DNS server, the browser cannot translate 'google.com' into an IP address. Fix: set DNS to 8.8.8.8 or 1.1.1.1 in the network adapter settings, or run ipconfig /flushdns to clear stale cache. The subnet mask /24 (255.255.255.0) is correct for this range, and the gateway 192.168.10.1 is in the same /24 subnet.

prompt: A network engineer needs to run a cable between two buildings 400 meters apart. Copper Ethernet will not work. Which cable type should be used?

options.text: Cat6a UTP
Cat8 STP
Fiber optic
Coaxial RG-6

explanation: All copper Ethernet is limited to 100 meters (Cat8 is 30 m). At 400 meters, only fiber optic cable can carry Ethernet signals. Fiber transmits light, not electrical signals, so it is also immune to electromagnetic interference (EMI) — ideal for running between buildings (where lightning strikes on copper can damage equipment) and through electrically noisy environments. Multi-mode fiber (MMF): up to ~550 m (OM4) using LED light, lower cost transceivers — good for 400 m. Single-mode fiber (SMF): up to tens of kilometers using laser light — overkill for 400 m but future-proof. Common fiber connectors: LC (small, data center standard), SC (square, push-pull), ST (bayonet, older installations).

prompt: Intel Core Ultra (LGA 1851) and AMD Ryzen 9000 (AM5) both use which socket type where the contact pins are located on the motherboard?

options.text: PGA — pins on the CPU
BGA — soldered to board
LGA — pins on the motherboard socket
ZIF — zero insertion force with pins on both

explanation: Both modern Intel (LGA 1851 for Core Ultra) and AMD AM5 (Ryzen 7000/9000) now use LGA (Land Grid Array) sockets where the pins are on the MOTHERBOARD and the CPU has flat contact pads (lands). A bent socket pin means an expensive motherboard repair. Historical context: AMD used PGA (pins on CPU) for AM4 (Ryzen 1000–5000) — bent CPU pins were more forgivable to fix. Intel has used LGA since LGA 775. BGA (Ball Grid Array): soldered permanently — laptops and mobile devices. For 220-1201: both current Intel and AMD desktop platforms now use LGA-style sockets, though they are not compatible with each other.

prompt: A technician installs an M.2 NVMe Gen 4 SSD. What approximate sequential read speed should this drive achieve?

options.text: 600 MB/s (SATA III max)
3,500 MB/s (NVMe Gen 3)
7,000 MB/s (NVMe Gen 4)
14,000 MB/s (NVMe Gen 5)

explanation: NVMe generational speeds (sequential read): Gen 3 (PCIe 3.0 x4): ~3,500 MB/s. Gen 4 (PCIe 4.0 x4): ~7,000 MB/s. Gen 5 (PCIe 5.0 x4): ~14,000 MB/s. SATA III: 600 MB/s hard ceiling. The M.2 form factor (2242, 2260, 2280) is just the physical size — it supports BOTH SATA and NVMe protocols. Check the drive label or spec sheet to determine which protocol is used. The motherboard slot must also support the correct PCIe generation for full speed (a Gen 4 NVMe in a Gen 3 slot runs at Gen 3 speed). For 220-1201, know all three NVMe generations and the SATA ceiling.

prompt: Which benefit does DDR5 have over DDR4 that improves memory reliability even in systems without a dedicated ECC controller?

options.text: DDR5 runs at higher voltage for stability
DDR5 includes on-die ECC built into each memory chip
DDR5 uses a narrower bus for less noise
DDR5 is backward compatible with DDR4 slots

explanation: DDR5 includes on-die ECC (Error-Correcting Code) within each individual memory chip — this is separate from system-level ECC (which requires a server motherboard and ECC DIMMs). On-die ECC detects and corrects single-bit errors within the memory chip itself before the data even leaves the module, improving stability for all DDR5 systems. Other DDR5 improvements: higher bandwidth (6400+ MT/s vs DDR4's 3200 MT/s), lower voltage (1.1V vs 1.2V), higher density (up to 128GB per DIMM), two independent 32-bit sub-channels per DIMM. DDR5 uses a different 288-pin slot with a notch in a different position — NOT backward compatible with DDR4.

prompt: A laser printer produces pages where toner smears when rubbed with a finger immediately after printing. Which stage of the laser printing process has failed?

options.text: Charging — drum not getting negative charge
Exposing — laser not drawing the image
Fusing — heat and pressure not bonding toner to paper
Developing — toner not adhering to drum

explanation: Fusing is Stage 6: heat rollers (~180°C) and pressure rollers permanently melt toner into the paper fibers. A failing fuser (broken heating element, worn rollers) means toner sits loose on the paper surface — it smears when touched. Test: rub your finger on a freshly printed page — if it smears, replace the fuser. Full 7-stage laser printing process: 1-Processing (RIP), 2-Charging (drum gets -600V uniform charge), 3-Exposing (laser neutralizes charged areas to form latent image), 4-Developing (toner attaches to exposed areas), 5-Transferring (paper gets positive charge, attracts toner), 6-Fusing (heat bonds toner permanently), 7-Cleaning (residual toner removed from drum). Know every stage and what failure looks like.

prompt: A PC has absolutely no signs of life — no fans, no LEDs, no beeps. The wall outlet is confirmed working. What is the FIRST component to test?

options.text: RAM
CPU
PSU (Power Supply Unit)
GPU

explanation: When a PC shows zero signs of life (no fans, no LEDs, no display, no beeps), the PSU is the first suspect because it powers every other component. A completely failed PSU means nothing else can receive power to operate. PSU test: use a PSU tester, or the paperclip test (short the PS_ON green wire to a ground/black wire on the 24-pin connector — if the PSU fan spins, the PSU has basic functionality). If PSU passes: check the wall outlet again, check the power cable, check the front panel power switch connector on the motherboard. RAM or CPU failures typically cause POST failures — system powers on (fans spin, LEDs light) but fails to boot, often with beep codes.

prompt: Which display connector standard carries both digital video AND audio in a single cable and is the most common connector on consumer televisions and monitors?

options.text: VGA (DB-15)
DVI-D
HDMI
S-Video

explanation: HDMI (High-Definition Multimedia Interface) carries both digital video and audio in one cable — no separate audio cable needed. HDMI 2.1 supports 4K@120Hz, 8K, HDR10+, VRR (Variable Refresh Rate), and eARC. DisplayPort: digital video (and audio), higher max bandwidth than HDMI, used on PC monitors and laptops — DP 2.1 supports up to 16K. USB-C/Thunderbolt: can carry DisplayPort Alt Mode signal plus power and data. VGA (DB-15): analog video only, no audio, 15-pin D-Sub connector — obsolete, limited resolution. DVI-D: digital video only, no audio — mostly replaced. DVI-I: carries both analog and digital but still no audio. For the exam: HDMI = video + audio on one cable.

prompt: A company uses Microsoft 365 for email and Office apps hosted entirely by Microsoft with no on-premises servers to manage. Which cloud service model is this?

options.text: IaaS
PaaS
SaaS
DaaS

explanation: SaaS (Software as a Service): the provider manages everything — hardware, OS, middleware, and the application. The customer only manages their data and user access. Examples: Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Salesforce, Dropbox, Zoom, Adobe Creative Cloud. IaaS: provider delivers virtualized infrastructure (compute, storage, networking); customer manages OS and above. Examples: AWS EC2, Azure VMs. PaaS: provider manages infrastructure and runtime; customer manages application code and data. Examples: Azure App Service, AWS Lambda, Google App Engine. DaaS (Desktop as a Service): virtual desktops from the cloud. Examples: Amazon WorkSpaces, Azure Virtual Desktop — useful for remote workers, thin clients, kiosk deployments.

prompt: VMware ESXi runs directly on server hardware with no host OS installed beneath it. This is a Type ___ hypervisor, and it is preferred in production because:

options.text: Type 2; it is easier to configure
Type 1; it has direct hardware access for better performance and security
Type 1; it supports more guest OS types
Type 2; it requires less specialized hardware

explanation: Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisors run DIRECTLY on physical hardware with no host OS layer — direct hardware access delivers better performance, efficiency, and a smaller attack surface. Examples: VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V (server), Proxmox VE, Xen, KVM. Standard in data centers and enterprise. Type 2 (hosted) hypervisors run as applications on top of a host OS. The host OS mediates hardware access — adding overhead and attack surface. Examples: Oracle VirtualBox, VMware Workstation/Fusion, Parallels Desktop. Used for developer workstations, testing labs, and desktop virtualization. For 220-1201: Type 1 = enterprise/server; Type 2 = desktop/personal use.

prompt: A web app automatically provisions additional cloud servers during a product launch traffic spike, then releases them when demand drops — paying only for actual usage. Which two NIST cloud characteristics does this describe?

options.text: Multi-tenancy and SLA
Broad network access and private cloud
Rapid elasticity and measured service
On-demand self-service and resource pooling

explanation: NIST defines five essential cloud characteristics: 1. On-demand self-service: provision resources without provider interaction. 2. Broad network access: accessible over any network. 3. Resource pooling: provider resources shared across customers. 4. Rapid elasticity: scale resources up or down quickly and automatically. 5. Measured service: usage is metered, billed per consumption (pay-per-use). Auto-scaling during traffic spikes = rapid elasticity. Pay-only-for-what-you-use = measured service. Together they enable cost-efficient handling of variable workloads — a major cloud advantage over fixed on-premises infrastructure. Containers (Docker/Kubernetes) enable rapid elasticity at the application layer by spinning up/down containers in seconds.

prompt: A DevOps team deploys 50 microservices using Docker containers on a single Linux host. How do containers differ from running 50 virtual machines on the same host?

options.text: Containers each run a full OS; VMs share the host kernel
Containers share the host OS kernel and are far lighter; VMs each include a full OS via a hypervisor
Both are identical in resource usage and isolation
Containers use Type 1 hypervisors; VMs use Type 2

explanation: Containers share the host OS kernel — they package only the application and its dependencies. This makes them much lighter (MBs vs GBs), start in seconds (vs minutes for VMs), and pack many more instances on the same hardware. Trade-off: less isolation than VMs — a kernel vulnerability could affect all containers on that host. Virtual Machines each include a complete guest OS running on a hypervisor — stronger isolation, larger footprint, slower to start. Use containers for: microservices, CI/CD pipelines, rapid deployment, cloud-native apps. Use VMs for: strong isolation requirements, running different OS families on same hardware, legacy app compatibility. Docker: container runtime. Kubernetes: orchestrates containers across clusters at scale.

prompt: A desktop PC is making a repetitive clicking noise from inside. The user is in the middle of a project. What should the technician do FIRST?

options.text: Run a defragmentation utility to fix the issue
Immediately back up all critical data — the hard drive is failing
Reformat and reinstall Windows
Replace the CPU cooling fan

explanation: The 'click of death' — a rhythmic clicking from a mechanical HDD — means the read/write heads are failing to find their home position and resetting. This indicates imminent and total physical failure that can happen within minutes. DATA PRESERVATION is the only priority. Copy all critical files to another drive or cloud storage immediately. Every additional read/write operation on a failing drive risks accelerating the failure and making data permanently unrecoverable. After securing data: replace the drive (ideally with an SSD), reinstall Windows, restore data from backup. A defrag writes heavily to the drive — extremely dangerous on a clicking drive. SSDs fail differently — SMART warnings usually precede failure. Always monitor SMART health data proactively.

prompt: A newly assembled PC powers on but emits a repeating single long beep and shows no video output. What does this beep pattern MOST likely indicate?

options.text: Successful POST — the system is ready
RAM not seated correctly or incompatible memory
Hard drive not detected
GPU driver needs updating

explanation: A continuous or repeating long beep at POST almost universally indicates a memory (RAM) error on AMI and Award BIOS systems. With no video and this beep pattern: 1. Power off completely. 2. Reseat RAM modules firmly — press until both retention clips snap. 3. Try one stick at a time in different slots. 4. Clear CMOS (jumper or remove battery for 30 seconds) to reset BIOS settings. 5. Test with known-good RAM. Beep code meanings vary by BIOS manufacturer — always check the motherboard manual. No beeps + no power = PSU or motherboard. No beeps + has power but no video = possible GPU issue. Multiple short beeps (3–5) = often GPU issues on certain BIOS implementations.

prompt: A laser printer produces pages with a faint repeated image appearing at regular intervals across the entire page — like a ghost of the previous print. Which component is MOST likely causing this?

options.text: Fuser assembly
Imaging drum
Toner cartridge level
Transfer corona wire

explanation: Ghosting — a faint repeated 'shadow' of previous content appearing at regular intervals matching the drum's circumference — is caused by a worn or damaged imaging drum that is not cleaning properly between rotations. Residual toner or charge from the previous cycle creates a faint impression on subsequent pages. The drum is the photosensitive cylinder that holds the electrostatic image before toner transfer. In many modern printers, the drum is integrated into the toner cartridge assembly — replacing the cartridge resolves both. Fuser issues: toner smears when touched (not bonded). Transfer corona issues: blank or very faint pages (toner not transferred). Toner cartridge depletion: gradually fading output, not repetitive ghost marks.

prompt: A laptop is connected to the network via Ethernet but shows IP address 169.254.88.15. Other devices on the same switch work fine. What does this IP indicate and what should be checked first?

options.text: The laptop has a static IP correctly set in this range
DHCP failed — the OS self-assigned an APIPA address. Check the DHCP lease and network connection
The laptop is connected to a secondary VLAN
The IP indicates the laptop is using IPv6

explanation: 169.254.0.0/16 is the APIPA (Automatic Private IP Addressing) range — Windows self-assigns an address here when it cannot reach a DHCP server within 60 seconds. APIPA hosts can only communicate with other APIPA devices on the same segment — no gateway, no internet, no domain resources. Since other devices work, the network itself is fine. The problem is specific to this laptop. Troubleshooting steps: 1. Check physical connection — is the link light on? 2. ipconfig /release then ipconfig /renew. 3. Check if the laptop's NIC has a manual/static configuration overriding DHCP. 4. Check if the DHCP scope has available addresses. 5. Try a different cable or switch port. 6. Check if a firewall on the laptop is blocking DHCP.

prompt: Users report slow Wi-Fi speeds during business hours but excellent speeds on evenings and weekends. AP signal strength is strong. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The AP firmware is outdated
Channel congestion from too many simultaneous users or neighboring APs on the same channel
The Ethernet uplink cable to the AP is faulty
DHCP scope exhaustion

explanation: The time-of-day pattern (slow during business hours when all users are present, fast when the office is empty) is the classic signature of channel congestion — too many devices competing for airtime on the same Wi-Fi channel. Solutions: Use a Wi-Fi analyzer (NetSpot, inSSIDer) to find the least congested channel. On 2.4 GHz use only channels 1, 6, or 11 (non-overlapping). Migrate heavy users to 5 GHz (more channels, less interference, shorter range). Enable band steering to automatically push 5 GHz-capable devices to 5 GHz. Deploy additional APs to reduce clients per AP. Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) with OFDMA dramatically improves performance in dense environments. Strong signal + slow speed = congestion problem, NOT a coverage problem.

prompt: An inkjet printer outputs pages with horizontal white lines and streaks through text and images. What is the MOST likely cause and first corrective action?

options.text: Replace the fuser assembly
Run the printhead nozzle cleaning utility to clear clogged ink nozzles
Replace all ink cartridges immediately
Adjust the paper thickness setting

explanation: Horizontal streaks (missing bands of color or white lines through output) in inkjet printing are the classic symptom of clogged print nozzles. Ink dries in the tiny nozzle openings when the printer sits unused. First action: run the built-in printhead cleaning utility (found in printer software under Maintenance, or on the printer control panel). Then print a nozzle check pattern to verify improvement. Multiple cleaning cycles may be needed for severe clogs. Only replace cartridges if ink levels are confirmed low — a nozzle check pattern helps identify which color is clogged. Prevention: print at least one page per week to keep nozzles from drying. Persistent clogs after multiple cleaning cycles may require manual head cleaning or printhead replacement.

prompt: A server running RAID 5 across four drives reports one drive failure. The array is still accessible. What is the CORRECT immediate action?

options.text: Shut the server down immediately to prevent data loss
The data is already lost — restore from backup
Replace the failed drive as soon as possible to restore parity and redundancy before a second drive fails
Convert the remaining three drives to RAID 0 for better performance

explanation: RAID 5 can survive exactly ONE drive failure — it continues operating in a degraded state, reconstructing data on the fly using parity. However in this state there is ZERO remaining redundancy — a second drive failure means complete data loss. The critical window between the first and second failure is dangerous: degraded array I/O stresses remaining drives, and rebuild reads stress them further (URE risk). Immediate actions: replace the failed drive immediately (use a hot spare if available for auto-rebuild). Monitor rebuild progress — it can take hours on large drives. Avoid heavy I/O workloads during rebuild. After rebuild completes: verify data integrity and consider upgrading to RAID 6 (survives 2 failures) for improved resilience. RAID is NOT a backup — always maintain separate backups.

prompt: A user’s wireless headphones will not reconnect to their laptop despite being fully charged and in range. Which step should be tried FIRST?

options.text: Toggle Bluetooth off and on, then remove and re-pair the device
Replace the headphones immediately
Update the laptop’s BIOS firmware
Disable Wi-Fi to eliminate 2.4 GHz interference

explanation: Bluetooth stack state can become stale or corrupted, causing pairing failures. The quickest fix is: toggle Bluetooth off/on in Settings, forget/remove the device from the paired list, put the headphones into pairing mode, and pair fresh. If this fails, check the Bluetooth adapter driver in Device Manager and update if outdated. Bluetooth 5.x includes improved 2.4 GHz coexistence mechanisms that significantly reduce Wi-Fi interference compared to older Bluetooth versions.

prompt: A laptop battery reports 35% capacity but immediately powers off when unplugged. What has MOST likely happened?

options.text: The charging cable is defective
The BIOS needs a firmware update to read battery level correctly
The battery has degraded and can no longer hold a real charge — it needs replacement
The RAM is causing incorrect battery readings

explanation: Lithium-ion batteries degrade over charge cycles. When a battery’s actual capacity drops below what the operating system reports, the battery drains almost instantly under real load. The OS still believes it holds 35%, but the actual capacity is near zero. Diagnosis: check Battery Report (Windows: powercfg /batteryreport) to see DESIGN CAPACITY vs FULL CHARGE CAPACITY — if full charge is significantly below design, the battery is worn out. MacBook users: About This Mac → System Information → Power → Cycle Count. High cycle count (over 500–1000 depending on model) means replacement time. Never operate a physically swollen lithium battery — that is a critical safety hazard.

prompt: A user switches from Android to iPhone and wants all contacts, calendar, and email on the new phone immediately. What is the MOST efficient method?

options.text: Manually retype all contacts
Export contacts to vCard (.vcf), email them, and import
Sync data to a cloud account (Google Workspace or Microsoft 365) and sign in on the new device
Use Bluetooth to transfer everything simultaneously

explanation: Cloud synchronization is the most efficient and reliable method for device migration. If contacts/calendar/email are synced to Google or Microsoft 365, simply signing in on the new iPhone immediately populates all data — no manual transfer needed. Apple’s Move to iOS app can also transfer data wirelessly over a direct Wi-Fi connection. Bluetooth transfers files between nearby devices but is too slow for bulk contact/calendar data and doesn’t work as a sync mechanism. Corporate MDM enrollment typically sets up email/calendar automatically.

prompt: A technician notices an older Android phone only supports Micro-USB while the user’s new laptop uses USB-C. What is needed to connect the phone to the laptop for data transfer?

options.text: A USB-C to Micro-USB adapter or cable
A Lightning to USB-A cable
A Thunderbolt 4 cable
A USB-A to USB-A cable

explanation: Micro-USB (standard on older Android) and USB-C (modern universal standard) are physically incompatible — a Micro-USB to USB-C adapter or a cable with Micro-USB on one end and USB-C on the other is required. Connector reference: USB-A: large rectangular connector on older computers. USB-B: square connector on printers. Micro-USB: small flat directional connector, previous Android standard. USB-C: reversible oval connector, modern universal standard on Android phones, iPads, MacBooks. Lightning: Apple proprietary, iPhones through iPhone 14; replaced by USB-C from iPhone 15. For the 220-1201: know ALL connector types, their devices, and that adapters bridge incompatible standards.

prompt: A workstation has IP 192.168.1.50/24 and default gateway 192.168.1.1. Can it communicate with 10.0.0.5 without a router?

options.text: Yes — all private IP addresses can communicate without a router
No — 10.0.0.5 is on a different network; the default gateway must route the traffic
Yes — if both devices are on the same physical switch
No — the workstation cannot communicate with any 10.x.x.x address under any circumstances

explanation: The workstation is on the 192.168.1.0/24 network. 10.0.0.5 belongs to 10.0.0.0/8 — a completely different IP network. Devices can only communicate directly (at Layer 2) when they share the same IP subnet. Communication between different subnets requires a router. The default gateway (192.168.1.1) routes packets to other networks. If the gateway is missing or incorrect, the workstation can still talk to devices on 192.168.1.0/24 but cannot reach anything outside that range.

prompt: A technician needs to connect a computer to the network via a wall port with 8 conductors. Which cable and connector standard should be used?

options.text: Coaxial RG-6
RJ-11 with 2 conductors
RJ-45 with Cat5e or better
ST fiber optic connector

explanation: Ethernet uses RJ-45 connectors (8-pin 8-conductor). RJ-11 is the 6-pin telephone connector and cannot carry Ethernet. Cat5e or better cable terminated with RJ-45 connectors is the standard for Ethernet LAN connections. Coaxial RG-6: used for cable TV and satellite — not standard Ethernet. Fiber optic connectors (ST, LC, SC): require an optical NIC or transceiver — most office ports are copper RJ-45. Cable category requirements: Cat5e for 1 Gbps; Cat6a for 10 Gbps at full 100 m.

prompt: A technician is setting up an AP in a 2.4 GHz-congested office. Adjacent APs use channels 1 and 6. Which channel should the new AP use to avoid overlap?

options.text: Channel 3
Channel 6
Channel 11
Channel 14

explanation: The 2.4 GHz band has only three non-overlapping channels in most regions: 1, 6, and 11. Each channel is 22 MHz wide but spaced 5 MHz apart — channels 2 through 5 overlap with both 1 and 6; channels 7 through 10 overlap with both 6 and 11. Using overlapping channels causes co-channel interference, dramatically reducing performance. If APs use 1 and 6, channel 11 is the only non-overlapping choice. Channel 14: available in Japan only — illegal in the US and most countries. 5 GHz has 24+ non-overlapping channels and is the preferred band for performance-sensitive use.

prompt: A company’s DHCP scope shows 0 available IP addresses, but only 40 of the 50 scoped devices are active. What is MOST likely causing this?

options.text: The router is not forwarding DHCP requests
DHCP lease times are too long and old leases from decommissioned devices have not expired
DNS is down and blocking DHCP responses
The switch is blocking all DHCP broadcasts

explanation: DHCP lease exhaustion with fewer active devices than scope size typically means old leases from retired or removed devices are still consuming addresses. When a device leaves gracefully it sends a DHCPRELEASE, freeing its lease. But devices that are simply unplugged or have their NICs replaced (new MAC = new lease) leave orphaned leases that consume space until they expire. Solutions: reduce lease duration, check the DHCP lease table for inactive MAC addresses and manually clear them, or increase the scope size. Guest/BYOD networks should use short lease times (1–2 hours) to recycle addresses quickly.

prompt: A small business needs a two-drive array providing full redundancy — if one drive fails the system keeps running. Which RAID level should be used?

options.text: RAID 0
RAID 1
RAID 5
JBOD

explanation: RAID 1 (mirroring) writes identical data to both drives simultaneously. If either drive fails, the other has a complete copy — the system keeps running with no data loss. Only two drives are needed. Usable capacity equals one drive (50% efficiency). RAID 0: stripes data across two drives for doubled performance, but if either fails ALL data is lost — zero redundancy. RAID 5: requires minimum 3 drives and cannot be implemented with only 2. JBOD: treats drives as independent volumes, no redundancy. For a simple two-drive redundancy requirement, RAID 1 is always the answer.

prompt: A technician boots a newly built PC and receives a POST error indicating BIOS settings were lost. The time and date are also wrong. Which component has MOST likely failed?

options.text: RAM module
CMOS battery (CR2032)
Hard drive
CPU

explanation: The CMOS battery (a CR2032 lithium coin cell) powers the CMOS memory that stores BIOS/UEFI settings (date/time, boot order, CPU settings) when the PC is unplugged. If the CMOS battery fails or dies (typically after 3–5+ years), settings revert to defaults at every power cycle. Symptoms: clock resets to Jan 1 1970 or 2000, BIOS settings lost repeatedly. Fix: replace the CR2032 battery (costs under $2), re-enter BIOS settings. You can also clear CMOS intentionally by removing the battery for 30 seconds or using the CLR_CMOS jumper on the motherboard — useful for recovering from bad BIOS settings that prevent booting.

prompt: A high-end workstation with a power-hungry GPU experiences random shutdowns under heavy load. Other systems on the same circuit work fine. What is MOST likely the cause?

options.text: The RAM is overheating
The monitor resolution is too high
The PSU wattage is insufficient for the system’s power demands under full load
The Ethernet cable is causing interference

explanation: A PSU that is underpowered works fine at idle (low power draw) but shuts down or reboots under full load when power demand spikes. Modern GPUs can draw 300–600W alone at full load. PSU sizing rule: calculate the total system TDP then add 20–30% headroom. Example: CPU 250W + GPU 450W + other 100W = 800W minimum; use a 1000–1200W PSU for headroom. 80 Plus rating (Bronze/Silver/Gold/Platinum/Titanium) indicates efficiency, not output capacity. Use PCPartPicker or manufacturer power estimator tools to calculate system requirements. Random shutdown under load + other systems unaffected = PSU capacity issue, not a circuit issue.

prompt: A technician replaces a CPU. After reassembly, the system immediately shuts down due to CPU overheating. What was MOST likely forgotten during installation?

options.text: Re-seating the RAM modules
Applying thermal paste between the CPU and heatsink
Updating the BIOS after CPU replacement
Reconnecting the SATA power cables

explanation: Thermal paste fills microscopic air gaps between the CPU IHS (Integrated Heat Spreader) and the heatsink base. Without thermal paste, air pockets dramatically increase thermal resistance, causing the CPU to overheat within seconds. Modern CPUs have automatic thermal shutdown to prevent damage — the shutdown IS the CPU self-protecting. Application: apply a pea-sized amount to the center of the CPU and let the heatsink spread it when mounted. Don’t apply too much — excess paste can spill onto the socket. Some heatsinks come with pre-applied compound. Liquid metal compounds offer better performance but are electrically conductive — handle carefully.

prompt: A small office needs a printer for high-volume archival-quality smudge-resistant black-and-white contracts. Which printer type is BEST?

options.text: Inkjet
Laser
Thermal (direct thermal)
Dot matrix (impact)

explanation: Laser printers are ideal for high-volume black-and-white text: dry toner is heat-fused to paper, producing smudge-resistant, water-resistant output. Fast print speeds (20–60+ ppm), low per-page cost at high volume, crisp text quality. Inkjet: liquid ink can smear when wet, slower for high volume, more expensive per page at high volumes, excellent for color/photo printing. Thermal (direct thermal): heat-sensitive paper, no separate ink/toner — used in receipt printers and shipping labels. Output fades over time, not suitable for contracts. Dot matrix (impact): uses ink ribbon and pins, very slow, noisy, produces carbon copies — used for multi-part NCR forms only.

prompt: A laptop’s documentation specifies its M.2 slot is ‘SATA only.’ The technician installs an M.2 NVMe Gen 4 drive. What will happen?

options.text: The NVMe drive will work at full Gen 4 speed
The NVMe drive will work at reduced SATA speed
The NVMe drive will not be recognized because the slot only supports the SATA protocol
The laptop will boot from the NVMe drive but only in legacy BIOS mode

explanation: M.2 is a PHYSICAL FORM FACTOR, not a protocol. An M.2 slot can support SATA protocol, NVMe/PCIe protocol, or both — depending on the motherboard/laptop design. An M.2 NVMe drive in a SATA-only M.2 slot will not be recognized because the protocols are incompatible (NVMe communicates over PCIe lanes; SATA uses a different controller). Always check the motherboard/laptop documentation BEFORE purchasing: does the M.2 slot support SATA, NVMe, or both? Physical key notch compatibility: NVMe drives typically use M-key; SATA M.2 drives use B+M key. ALWAYS verify protocol support, not just physical fit — this is a very common and expensive mistake.

prompt: A healthcare company needs cloud services but must ensure all patient data stays within its own controlled infrastructure due to HIPAA requirements. Which cloud deployment model is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Public cloud (AWS, Azure)
Community cloud
Private cloud
Hybrid cloud with public storage

explanation: A private cloud gives an organization dedicated cloud infrastructure — it can be on-premises or hosted at a provider but completely isolated for that single organization. Private cloud is appropriate when data sovereignty and compliance requirements (HIPAA, GDPR, classified data) are strict, or when the organization needs full control. Public cloud: infrastructure shared with other organizations (multi-tenant). Community cloud: shared between organizations with common requirements (e.g., multiple hospitals sharing a HIPAA-compliant cloud). Hybrid cloud: combination of private and public. For HIPAA workloads, major cloud providers offer HIPAA Business Associate Agreements (BAAs) and HIPAA-eligible services on public cloud — but strict configuration is required.

prompt: Before applying a major OS update to a VM, an administrator takes a snapshot. If the update causes problems, what does the snapshot enable?

options.text: Automatically patches the VM back on a schedule
Restores the VM to its exact state at the moment the snapshot was taken, undoing all changes
Backs up only the files changed during the update
Migrates the VM to a different host server

explanation: A VM snapshot captures the complete state of a virtual machine at a specific moment: disk contents, memory state, VM settings, and power state. If the OS update causes instability, reverting to the snapshot instantly restores the VM exactly as it was before — the update and all its changes are undone. Snapshots are ideal for: testing patches/updates, major configuration changes, risky software installations. Important limitations: snapshots are NOT backups — they share the same underlying storage as the VM. If the datastore fails, both the VM and snapshot are lost. Long-term snapshots significantly impact performance (delta files grow). Best practice: take snapshot, test, then delete the snapshot once satisfied.

prompt: A retail company experiences 10x normal traffic on Black Friday. Their cloud app automatically provisions 50 additional servers during peak and releases them afterward. Which two NIST cloud characteristics describe this?

options.text: Broad network access and private cloud
Multi-tenancy and SLA
Rapid elasticity and measured service
On-demand self-service only

explanation: Two NIST cloud characteristics work together here: Rapid elasticity: scale resources up quickly (50 servers added automatically) and release them when demand drops — resources appear unlimited to the consumer. Measured service: pay only for what you actually consume (metered billing) — those 50 extra servers cost money only during Black Friday, not year-round. Without elasticity, a retailer would need permanent infrastructure sized for peak demand, wasting money 364 days per year. Auto-scaling in AWS, Azure, and GCP implements rapid elasticity by monitoring metrics (CPU, requests/second) and automatically adding or removing instances. The five NIST cloud characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service.

prompt: A desktop PC runs fine for 30 minutes then suddenly powers off. After sitting for an hour it works fine again. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: RAM failure
Hard drive failure
CPU or system overheating causing thermal shutdown
Power supply failure under load

explanation: The pattern — works fine, progressively gets worse, shuts down, then works after a cool-down — is the classic signature of thermal shutdown. Investigation: open the case and check for dust-clogged heatsink/radiator (the #1 cause), dried-out thermal paste, blocked case airflow, failed or seized CPU fan. Fix: clean dust from heatsink and fans with compressed air, replace thermal paste, ensure all case fans are functional. If the system runs fine cold then progressively fails, temperature is the variable. A PSU failure typically causes immediate shutdown or no-post, not a progressive thermal pattern. RAM failure causes BSODs or memory errors, not thermal shutdown.

prompt: A newly assembled PC powers on (fans spin, LEDs light) but displays absolutely nothing on the monitor. The monitor works on another PC. What should the technician check FIRST?

options.text: Replace the CPU
Reinstall Windows
Verify the display cable is connected to the GPU output (not the motherboard) and that RAM is fully seated
Test with a different power supply

explanation: No display after a successful power-on (fans spin) is usually caused by: 1) Video output connected to the wrong port — if a discrete GPU is installed, the display cable must connect to the GPU, not the motherboard’s integrated video port (which is often disabled when a discrete GPU is present). 2) RAM not fully seated — if RAM is in the wrong slots or not clicked in, the system powers on but cannot POST and shows no video. Try reseating RAM in the recommended slots (check motherboard manual). Other causes: GPU not fully seated in PCIe slot, monitor input set to wrong source. Check for POST beep codes — they indicate which component is failing.

prompt: A user reports a paper jam but cannot find any paper inside. The printer still shows a jam error after clearing visible paper. What is the NEXT step?

options.text: Replace the printer immediately
Check for small torn paper fragments in the paper path and rollers that may be triggering the jam sensor
Run the printer’s self-test print
Update the printer firmware

explanation: A persistent jam message after the visible paper is removed is almost always caused by a small torn piece of paper left behind near a sensor or roller. Even a 1-inch fragment will keep the error active. Inspection steps: use a flashlight to check the entire paper path including rollers, duplexing unit (back door), output tray area, and fuser entry. Remove fragments with tweezers — never use sharp metal tools that could damage rollers. Power cycle after clearing. Worn pick rollers can also cause chronic jams — roller replacement is standard maintenance for high-volume printers. Always pull paper in the direction of the paper feed path, never backward — backward removal can damage the fuser.

prompt: A laptop displays a perfect image on an external monitor via HDMI, but the built-in screen shows only black. What has MOST likely failed?

options.text: The GPU has failed
The laptop’s LCD cable, backlight, or panel has failed
Windows display settings are incorrect
The BIOS needs to be updated

explanation: The key diagnostic: external monitor works perfectly. This proves the GPU, graphics driver, and Windows are all functional. The problem is isolated to the built-in display system. Common built-in laptop display failures: LCD cable (connects display to motherboard) — often damaged by opening/closing the lid thousands of times. Backlight failure (LED strips) — the image exists but is invisible without backlight; shine a flashlight at the screen at an angle to check for a dim image. Inverter failure (older CCFL backlights) — similar to backlight failure. LCD panel failure — dead pixels or completely black. Diagnosis tip: shine a bright flashlight at the screen — if you see a very dim image, it’s backlight/inverter. If nothing, it’s likely the cable or panel.

prompt: A user needs to connect their USB-C laptop to two external monitors, a wired keyboard, an Ethernet port, and a USB-A printer — all through a single cable. Which device makes this possible?

options.text: A USB-A hub — adds USB ports only
A Thunderbolt/USB-C docking station — expands a single USB-C port to multiple display and peripheral connections
A KVM switch — shares peripherals between multiple computers
A port replicator that requires a proprietary connector on the laptop base

explanation: A USB-C/Thunderbolt docking station connects via a single USB-C or Thunderbolt 3/4 cable and provides: multiple USB-A and USB-C ports, HDMI/DisplayPort outputs (often 2 or more), Ethernet (RJ-45), audio jacks, SD card reader, and power delivery (charges the laptop through the same cable). Thunderbolt 4 docks support up to two 4K displays, 40 Gbps data, and 100W charging simultaneously. USB-C docks without Thunderbolt are more limited — check the laptop's maximum supported display count. USB-A hubs only add USB-A ports and cannot carry video. KVM switches let one set of peripherals control multiple computers — the opposite use case. Proprietary port replicators (older HP/Lenovo docking stations) require a specific connector on the laptop base — not USB-C based.

prompt: A new employee needs to configure corporate email on their iPhone. IT provides: Exchange server address, domain\username, and password. Which email protocol should be used for Exchange integration with a full calendar and contacts sync?

options.text: POP3 — downloads messages to device only
IMAP — syncs email folders but not calendar/contacts
Microsoft Exchange ActiveSync (EAS) — syncs email, calendar, contacts, and tasks
SMTP — outbound mail delivery only

explanation: Microsoft Exchange ActiveSync (EAS) is the mobile protocol designed for Exchange environments. It syncs: email (with server-side push delivery), calendar, contacts, tasks, and notes — all bidirectionally between the device and Exchange server. If a meeting is added on the phone, it immediately appears in Outlook on the PC and vice versa. POP3: downloads messages to the device, marks them read on server (or deletes), no bidirectional sync, no calendar/contacts. IMAP: syncs email folders bidirectionally but does not sync calendar or contacts. SMTP: only for sending outbound email — never used to receive. iOS native Mail app supports EAS directly: Settings → Mail → Add Account → Microsoft Exchange → enter server/credentials. Corporate environments may require an MDM-enrolled profile that configures EAS automatically.

prompt: A company policy requires all corporate smartphones to lock after 30 seconds of inactivity and require a PIN or fingerprint to unlock. Which MDM setting enforces these requirements?

options.text: Remote wipe — erases the device if it is lost
Device passcode policy with maximum auto-lock timeout enforced via MDM
App whitelisting — restricts which apps can be installed
Container policy — creates a separate encrypted work profile

explanation: MDM (Mobile Device Management) platforms like Microsoft Intune, Jamf, or VMware Workspace ONE allow IT to push a device passcode policy that: requires a minimum PIN length or complexity, enables biometric unlock (fingerprint, Face ID), and enforces a maximum auto-lock timeout (30 seconds in this case). If the user tries to set a longer timeout, the device rejects it and resets to the MDM-enforced value. Remote wipe: deletes all data on a lost/stolen device — a different policy. App whitelisting: controls which applications can be installed. Container policy (Android Work Profile, iOS Managed Apps): separates corporate apps from personal apps in a secure container — a different feature. All of these MDM policies can coexist and are deployed simultaneously as a device compliance profile.

prompt: A passenger enables Airplane Mode on their phone before boarding. After landing, they want to use Bluetooth headphones but keep cellular off. What should they do?

options.text: Turn off Airplane Mode — all wireless functions return together
Keep Airplane Mode on and manually re-enable Bluetooth through the Control Center or Settings
Airplane Mode cannot be customized — cellular and Bluetooth always toggle together
Restart the phone to restore individual wireless toggles

explanation: Airplane Mode disables all wireless radios simultaneously (cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS). However, on both iOS and Android, you can manually re-enable individual wireless functions while keeping Airplane Mode on: swipe to Control Center (iOS) or Quick Settings (Android) and tap the Bluetooth icon. The device remembers this preference — on future flights, Airplane Mode on with Bluetooth manually re-enabled persists until changed. This is the standard setup for using wireless headphones or a Bluetooth keyboard on a flight. Wi-Fi can also be re-enabled on flights that offer inflight Wi-Fi while keeping cellular off. Airlines allow Bluetooth and Wi-Fi but require cellular (especially cellular voice) to be disabled during flight.

prompt: A corporate IT team deploys iPhones for executives and Android phones for field staff. Which statement accurately describes a key difference between iOS and Android for enterprise deployment?

options.text: Android does not support MDM enrollment — it can only be managed manually
iOS uses a curated App Store with Apple review; Android supports sideloading APKs by default without a store review process
iOS supports full filesystem access for users; Android restricts all file access
Both platforms are identical in their enterprise management capabilities

explanation: iOS vs Android key differences: App distribution: iOS requires apps to come from the App Store (Apple-reviewed) or via MDM enterprise distribution — sideloading unsigned apps is not possible on standard iOS. Android allows APK sideloading by enabling 'Unknown sources' or 'Install unknown apps' — apps can be installed outside the Play Store (higher malware risk). MDM support: both iOS and Android support MDM (Apple Business Manager + Intune for iOS; Android Enterprise for Android). iOS MDM (via Apple DEP/ABM): enrollment can be forced during Setup Assistant on corporate-issued iPhones — users cannot skip it. Android Enterprise: Work Profile (BYOD) or fully managed device mode for corporate devices. Fragmentation: Android has many manufacturers and OS versions — creating consistency challenges. iOS has one manufacturer and controlled update cadence.

prompt: An iPhone user is replacing their phone. They want to transfer all apps, settings, photos, and messages to the new iPhone with minimal manual setup. What is the MOST efficient method?

options.text: Manually reinstall every app from the App Store on the new phone
Use iCloud backup or iTunes/Finder backup to restore the full device to the new iPhone
Email all contacts to themselves and download photos to a computer
Use Bluetooth to transfer apps between phones

explanation: Apple's backup and restore ecosystem: iCloud Backup: backs up over Wi-Fi to iCloud (apps, settings, messages, photos if iCloud Photo Library is enabled, app data). On the new iPhone: sign in with Apple ID during setup → Restore from iCloud Backup → all content restores automatically. iTunes/Finder Backup (Mac or PC): encrypted local backup includes everything including Health data and passwords. On new iPhone: connect to computer → Restore from Backup. Quick Start: if both phones are available simultaneously, Quick Start wirelessly transfers settings and data directly phone-to-phone using peer-to-peer Wi-Fi — the fastest method when both devices are present. Bluetooth: too slow for app transfer and cannot transfer iOS apps (only contacts, photos in some cases). Android equivalent: Google One backup restores to a new Android device. Samsung Smart Switch: transfers data between Samsung devices.

prompt: A delivery driver's navigation app shows their location correctly outdoors but loses GPS signal completely inside a warehouse. Which technology can provide approximate indoor location when GPS is unavailable?

options.text: Bluetooth GPS — extends GPS signal indoors using Bluetooth repeaters
Assisted GPS (A-GPS) using Wi-Fi positioning and cellular tower triangulation
The device's compass — magnetic north can substitute for GPS
NFC — provides centimeter-level positioning indoors

explanation: GPS requires line-of-sight to multiple satellites — walls, roofs, and dense materials block satellite signals. Alternatives for indoor/limited-GPS environments: Wi-Fi Positioning: the device scans for nearby Wi-Fi networks and compares their SSIDs and signal strengths against a database (Google, Apple) of known Wi-Fi access point locations — provides room-level accuracy (10-30 meters). Cellular triangulation: measures signal strength from nearby cell towers — provides neighborhood-level accuracy (100-1000 meters). A-GPS (Assisted GPS): uses cellular/Wi-Fi to quickly download satellite ephemeris data, speeding up GPS acquisition when outdoors — not an indoor solution by itself. Bluetooth beacons (BLE): used in retail stores for indoor positioning (requires specific infrastructure — not standard). NFC: range is under 4 cm — useless for navigation. The compass only shows direction, not position.

prompt: A remote worker needs their smartphone to securely access the company's internal file server while traveling. IT provides a VPN profile. After installing the VPN on iOS, what must the user do each time they need access?

options.text: Nothing — the VPN connects automatically whenever any app needs it
Connect to the VPN through Settings or the VPN client app, authenticate, then access internal resources
Restart the phone before every VPN session
Switch to a specific carrier network first

explanation: Mobile VPN setup and usage: Installation: IT pushes a VPN configuration profile via MDM (automatic) or the user installs a VPN app (Cisco AnyConnect, Palo Alto GlobalProtect, Zscaler, etc.) and imports a profile. Manual connection: Settings → VPN → toggle On, or open the VPN app → Connect → authenticate (username/password, MFA). On-Demand VPN (iOS/Android): MDM can configure the VPN to connect automatically when accessing specific domains (e.g., company.internal) — so-called per-app VPN or always-on VPN. This requires MDM-managed configuration. Without on-demand rules, the user must manually connect. Per-App VPN: a corporate VPN that activates only when specific work apps (Outlook, Teams, SAP) are in use — personal browsing does not go through the VPN. The prompt asks about standard VPN use without automatic configuration, so manual connection is the answer.

prompt: A user's new smartphone supports wireless charging but is not charging when placed on a wireless charging pad. What should be checked first?

options.text: Replace the charging pad — it is incompatible with all Android devices
Ensure the phone is properly centered on the pad (coil alignment), the case is not too thick/metallic, and the pad has power
Disable Bluetooth — it interferes with wireless charging
Install a wireless charging app from the Play Store

explanation: Wireless charging uses inductive coupling between coils in the pad and the phone. Common failure causes: Coil misalignment: the transmitter and receiver coils must overlap — moving the phone even slightly off-center breaks the connection. Thick or metallic case: metal cases block magnetic fields and prevent charging. Cases over 3mm thick may also reduce efficiency. No power to the pad: verify the pad's USB-C/Micro-USB power cable is connected and the power adapter is working. Wrong standard: Qi is the universal wireless charging standard supported by iPhone 8+, most Android flagships. Some Samsung devices support faster proprietary wireless charging (15W) that requires a Samsung-branded pad. MagSafe (Apple): uses magnets to align the charger perfectly on iPhone 12+ — solves the alignment problem. Bluetooth does not interfere with wireless charging — it operates at different frequencies. There is no 'wireless charging app' — it is hardware-only.

prompt: A technician configures a firewall to allow web traffic. HTTP uses port 80. HTTPS uses port _____.
explanation: Critical port numbers for the 220-1201 exam — memorize all of these: 20/21: FTP (data/control). 22: SSH. 23: Telnet. 25: SMTP (email sending). 53: DNS. 67/68: DHCP (server/client). 80: HTTP. 110: POP3. 143: IMAP. 443: HTTPS (HTTP over TLS). 3389: RDP (Remote Desktop). 445: SMB (Windows file sharing). 137-139: NetBIOS. 161/162: SNMP (queries/traps). 389: LDAP. 636: LDAPS. 123: NTP. HTTPS (443) encrypts web traffic using TLS, providing confidentiality and authentication. Port 8080 and 8443 are common alternative HTTP/HTTPS ports used when the standard ports are blocked or in use — but 443 is the standard HTTPS port. Firewalls typically block all inbound ports by default and must explicitly allow port 80 and 443 for web servers.

prompt: A developer needs to securely transfer source code files to a Linux server without the files being transmitted in cleartext. Which protocol and port should be used?

options.text: FTP on port 21 — fast but transfers in plaintext
TFTP on port 69 — simple file transfer without authentication
SFTP on port 22 — Secure File Transfer Protocol runs over SSH
SMB on port 445 — Windows file sharing protocol

explanation: File transfer protocol comparison: FTP (port 20/21): username, password, and file contents transmitted in cleartext — never use on untrusted networks. TFTP (port 69 UDP): Trivial FTP — no authentication, no encryption, no directory listing. Used for network device config file transfers, PXE boot, and VOIP phone provisioning on trusted LANs. SFTP (port 22): Secure FTP — uses SSH for full encryption of authentication and data. Not related to FTP despite the name — a completely different protocol. SCP (port 22): Secure Copy — also uses SSH, simpler than SFTP but less feature-rich. FTPS (port 990/989 or port 21 with STARTTLS): FTP over TLS — adds encryption to standard FTP. SMB (port 445): Windows/Samba file sharing — not designed for developer deployments to Linux. For secure file transfer to Linux: SFTP or SCP (both use port 22 SSH).

prompt: A network administrator reviews a configuration and sees the address fe80::1c2d:3e4f:5a6b:7c8d. What type of address is this and how was it configured?

options.text: An IPv4 address in hexadecimal notation — manually assigned
An IPv6 link-local address — automatically self-configured on every IPv6-enabled interface using the fe80::/10 prefix
An IPv6 global unicast address — assigned by DHCP from an ISP
An IPv6 loopback address — equivalent to 127.0.0.1

explanation: IPv6 address format review: 128 bits written as 8 groups of 4 hexadecimal digits separated by colons. fe80::/10 is the link-local prefix — addresses starting with fe80 are ALWAYS link-local. Self-configuration: every IPv6-enabled interface automatically generates its own link-local address using EUI-64 (derived from the MAC address) or a random identifier — no DHCP or manual configuration needed. Link-local addresses: only valid on the local link segment (cannot be routed), used for neighbor discovery, router discovery, and initial communication. IPv6 address types: ::1 — loopback (equivalent to 127.0.0.1). fe80::/10 — link-local (auto-configured, non-routable). fc00::/7 (fd00::/8) — unique local (private, not internet-routable, like RFC 1918). 2000::/3 — global unicast (internet-routable, assigned by ISPs). ff00::/8 — multicast.

prompt: A small office uses the network 192.168.5.0/24. How many usable host addresses does this subnet provide?

options.text: 256 — all addresses in the range
254 — subtract 1 for network and 1 for broadcast addresses
255 — subtract only the broadcast address
252 — /24 wastes 4 addresses for routing

explanation: Subnetting formula: Total addresses = 2^(32-prefix) = 2^(32-24) = 2^8 = 256 addresses. Usable hosts = Total - 2 = 256 - 2 = 254. The two reserved addresses: Network address: 192.168.5.0 — identifies the subnet itself, cannot be assigned to a device. Broadcast address: 192.168.5.255 — sends packets to all hosts on the subnet, cannot be assigned to a device. So usable range is 192.168.5.1 through 192.168.5.254 = 254 hosts. Common subnet quick reference: /24 = 256 total, 254 usable. /25 = 128 total, 126 usable. /26 = 64 total, 62 usable. /27 = 32 total, 30 usable. /28 = 16 total, 14 usable. /29 = 8 total, 6 usable. /30 = 4 total, 2 usable (point-to-point links). /32 = 1 address (host route, loopback). The A+ exam tests basic /24 and /16 subnetting.

prompt: A company uses a proxy server to filter employee internet access, log web requests, and cache frequently visited websites. What OSI layer does a web proxy primarily operate at?

options.text: Layer 2 (Data Link) — inspects MAC addresses
Layer 3 (Network) — routes IP packets
Layer 7 (Application) — inspects and forwards HTTP/HTTPS content
Layer 4 (Transport) — inspects TCP/UDP port numbers only

explanation: A web proxy server operates at the Application layer (Layer 7) because it understands HTTP/HTTPS — the actual content of web requests. The proxy intercepts browser requests, makes the request on behalf of the client, and returns the response. Functions: Content filtering: blocks URLs, categories (social media, gambling), or specific keywords. Caching: stores copies of popular web content — subsequent requests are served from cache, reducing bandwidth and improving speed. Logging/monitoring: records every URL visited, timestamps, and data volume per user. Authentication: requires login before granting internet access. SSL inspection: decrypts HTTPS to inspect encrypted content (requires certificate installation on clients). Transparent proxy: clients have no proxy configured — traffic is intercepted at the network level. Explicit proxy: clients configure the proxy address in their browser or OS settings. Reverse proxy: sits in front of web servers, distributing requests to multiple backend servers.

prompt: A sales rep works from home and needs to securely access the company's internal CRM system using a web browser without installing a separate VPN client application. Which VPN type supports browser-based clientless access?

options.text: Site-to-site IPsec VPN — connects two office networks
SSL/TLS VPN (clientless) — accessed through a web browser using HTTPS
PPTP VPN — oldest VPN protocol, requires client software
L2TP/IPsec VPN — requires a dedicated VPN client

explanation: VPN types for the 220-1201: Site-to-site VPN (IPsec): connects two entire networks (e.g., main office to branch office) — routers handle the tunnel, individual users don't need clients. Remote access VPN: connects individual users to the corporate network. Client-based: requires installing a VPN client (Cisco AnyConnect, Palo Alto GlobalProtect, OpenVPN). SSL/TLS VPN (clientless): users access a web portal via HTTPS — the portal proxies access to internal resources. No client install required — just a modern web browser. Ideal for contractors, BYOD devices, or users who can't install software. PPTP: obsolete and broken — uses MPPE encryption which has known vulnerabilities. Never use on modern networks. L2TP/IPsec: common but requires a VPN client. IKEv2/IPsec: modern, fast, supports MOBIKE (seamless switching between Wi-Fi and cellular) — used by iOS and Windows native VPN.

prompt: A cable tester reports a 'crossed pair' error on a Cat6 run. What does this indicate and how does it differ from a split pair?

options.text: Crossed pair: the entire cable is wired as a crossover cable. Split pair: two wires from different pairs are swapped, which passes a basic continuity test but causes crosstalk
Both terms mean the same thing — the wiring colors are in the wrong order
Crossed pair: the cable is too long. Split pair: the cable has a break in one wire
Crossed pair: wrong connector type used. Split pair: wrong cable category installed

explanation: Cable wiring faults: Crossed pair: a pair of wires is swapped between pin positions (e.g., pins 1-2 connected to pins 3-6). A basic cable tester detects this by comparing pin-to-pin continuity. Open: a wire is broken — no continuity. Short: two wires touch — both show conductivity. Reversed pair: both wires of a pair are connected but polarity is reversed (1↔2 swapped within the pair). Split pair: wires from different pairs are swapped in a way that maintains the correct pin-to-pin continuity — a basic continuity tester PASSES this fault because all 8 pins connect correctly. However, a professional cable certifier FAILS it because the twisted pairs are no longer together, causing excessive crosstalk and signal degradation at high speeds. Split pairs are the most dangerous fault because they are invisible to simple testers. Diagnosis requires a cable certifier that measures NEXT (near-end crosstalk) to detect split pairs.

prompt: A company wants to prevent unmanaged personal devices from connecting to the corporate wired Ethernet network while allowing only IT-approved devices. Which technology enforces this at the switch port level?

options.text: VLAN segmentation alone — assigns devices to different VLANs based on port location
Port security with MAC address filtering — limits which MAC addresses can use a port
802.1X NAC (Network Access Control) — requires devices to authenticate via RADIUS before the port forwards traffic
DHCP reservation — only assigns IP addresses to known MAC addresses

explanation: 802.1X Network Access Control (NAC) is the most secure solution: When a device plugs into a switch port, the port sends no traffic (except EAPOL authentication frames). The device (supplicant) must authenticate using a certificate, username/password, or machine credential via EAP. The switch (authenticator) contacts a RADIUS server (authentication server) to verify credentials. If authentication succeeds: the switch opens the port and optionally places the device in the correct VLAN (based on identity). If authentication fails: the device gets no access or is placed in a quarantine VLAN. Port security (MAC filtering): only allows specific MAC addresses on a port — can be bypassed by MAC spoofing (trivial with software tools). DHCP reservation: only affects IP assignment — a device can still communicate at Layer 2 without an IP. VLANs: segregate traffic but don't authenticate devices. 802.1X is the enterprise-grade solution that cannot be defeated by MAC spoofing because it requires valid credentials.

prompt: A technician wants to add a 10 Gbps NIC to a server. The NIC requires a PCIe x4 slot. The motherboard has PCIe x16, x8, x4, and x1 slots available. Which slots can physically accept the NIC?

options.text: Only the PCIe x4 slot — PCIe cards must exactly match their slot size
PCIe x4, x8, and x16 slots — larger slots are backward compatible and can accept smaller cards
Only PCIe x16 — the largest slot accepts all card sizes
PCIe x1 and x4 only — x8 and x16 have different voltage requirements

explanation: PCIe slot compatibility: PCIe slots use mechanical sizing (x1, x4, x8, x16) based on the number of lanes. A smaller card ALWAYS fits in a larger slot (physical compatibility). A PCIe x4 card fits in x4, x8, or x16 slots — the card uses only the lanes it needs (x4) and the extra lanes are unused. Performance: the card operates at its maximum spec (x4) regardless of the larger slot. A PCIe x1 card fits in any slot (x1, x4, x8, x16). A PCIe x16 card only fits in x16 and very few x8 slots with open-ended connectors. Mechanical vs electrical: physically larger slots sometimes have fewer active lanes (e.g., an x16 physical slot wired with only x4 electrical lanes for cost savings). Check motherboard manual for actual lane counts. PCIe generations (speed per lane): Gen 3: 985 MB/s per lane. Gen 4: 1969 MB/s per lane. Gen 5: 3938 MB/s per lane. x4 Gen 3 = ~3.9 GB/s — sufficient for 10 Gbps NICs.

prompt: A user wants to build the smallest possible gaming PC that still supports a full-sized GPU and one NVMe SSD. Which motherboard form factor is MOST appropriate?

options.text: ATX — standard full-size, up to 7 expansion slots
Micro-ATX (mATX) — smaller than ATX, typically 4 expansion slots
Mini-ITX (mITX) — compact, 1 PCIe x16 slot for GPU, supports NVMe M.2
SSI EEB — server form factor with maximum expansion

explanation: Motherboard form factors and their dimensions: ATX: 305×244mm — standard for mid/full-tower cases. 7 expansion slots. Most connectivity options. Best for high-end builds. Micro-ATX: 244×244mm — fits mid-tower and some mini-tower cases. 4 expansion slots. Good balance of size and expandability. Mini-ITX: 170×170mm — smallest standard consumer form factor. 1 PCIe x16 slot (GPU), 1 or 2 M.2 slots, 2 RAM slots. Requires a specific mini-ITX case. ITX GPUs may need low-profile or must verify case GPU length clearance. E-ATX: Extended ATX (305×330mm+) — enthusiast platforms with multiple PCIe slots for multi-GPU, HEDT systems. SSI EEB (305×330mm): server/workstation form factor. The scenario asks for smallest possible gaming PC with GPU support and NVMe — Mini-ITX fits exactly: 1 full-PCIe x16 slot for any GPU + M.2 NVMe slot + small footprint case (Lian Li A4, Dan A4, etc.).

prompt: A PC running Windows crashes with random BSODs (Blue Screen of Death) at different times with different stop codes. A technician suspects RAM. Which tool is BEST to diagnose defective RAM?

options.text: chkdsk /r — scans the hard drive for bad sectors
MemTest86 — boots independently and runs comprehensive read/write tests on all RAM
sfc /scannow — checks Windows system files for corruption
Device Manager — shows hardware errors and missing drivers

explanation: MemTest86 is the gold standard for RAM testing: it boots from a USB drive (no OS required), tests all installed RAM with multiple read/write patterns across the entire address space, and reports any errors. Finding even one error indicates defective RAM that must be replaced. RAM failure symptoms: random BSODs with varying stop codes (not always the same error), system crashes during memory-intensive tasks, blue screens with codes like PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA (0x50), MEMORY_MANAGEMENT (0x1A), or IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL (0x0A). Troubleshooting steps: 1) Run MemTest86 for multiple passes (at minimum 2 full passes). 2) Test one stick at a time to isolate the bad module. 3) Try each stick in different slots (isolates bad slots on motherboard). Windows Memory Diagnostic: built into Windows (mdsched.exe) — less comprehensive than MemTest86 but accessible without a bootable USB. chkdsk: checks the disk, not RAM. sfc: checks Windows files, not hardware.

prompt: A user reports their screen shows corrupted graphics — random colored pixels, geometric artifacts, and occasional black screens — especially during gaming. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The monitor cable is loose — reseating it will fix the corruption
The GPU is overheating, failing, or the driver is corrupted — check temperatures and update/reinstall drivers
The hard drive is failing — run SMART diagnostics
The RAM has a bad module — run MemTest86

explanation: GPU artifacts (pixel corruption, geometric shapes, texture glitches) are the classic symptoms of: GPU overheating: check GPU temperature with GPU-Z or MSI Afterburner. Normal gaming temps: 65-85°C. Over 95°C consistently = overheating. Clean GPU heatsink, replace thermal pads if cooler is old. GPU driver corruption/conflict: uninstall driver with DDU (Display Driver Uninstaller) in Safe Mode, then install the latest driver from NVIDIA/AMD. Failing GPU: GPU VRAM (Video RAM) degradation causes persistent artifacts that worsen over time. Test with a different GPU to confirm.
