Overclocked GPU: unstable OC settings cause artifacts — reset to stock clock speeds. Driver issue artifacts: usually software-consistent (specific games, resolutions). Hardware failure artifacts: usually random and worsen over time. Monitor cable artifacts: typically single-color lines or missing pixel rows, not geometric corruption. Hard drive issues: cause system freezes, boot failures — not graphical artifacts. RAM issues: cause BSODs, not graphical corruption.

prompt: Which storage interface uses a 7-pin data cable and a 15-pin power cable and is the standard connection for 2.5-inch laptop HDDs and optical drives?

options.text: NVMe — uses the M.2 form factor with no separate cables
SATA (Serial ATA) — uses a 7-pin data cable and 15-pin power connector
PATA/IDE — uses a 40/80-conductor ribbon cable and 4-pin Molex power
SAS (Serial Attached SCSI) — enterprise storage interface

explanation: Storage interface comparison: SATA (Serial ATA): 7-pin L-shaped data cable, 15-pin power connector. Speeds: SATA I (1.5 Gbps), SATA II (3 Gbps), SATA III (6 Gbps = 600 MB/s). Used for: 2.5-inch and 3.5-inch HDDs, SSDs, optical drives (Blu-ray, DVD). PATA/IDE (Parallel ATA): 40 or 80-conductor ribbon cable, 4-pin Molex power. Obsolete — found only in very old systems. Speeds: 33-133 MB/s (ATA/33 through ATA/133). M.2 NVMe: no separate cables — directly slots into M.2 connector on motherboard. PCIe interface. Speeds up to 7000+ MB/s (Gen 4). M.2 SATA: M.2 form factor using SATA protocol — limited to 600 MB/s. SAS: enterprise server HDDs — 12 Gbps, more reliable than SATA, backward compatible with SATA drives. U.2 (formerly SFF-8639): enterprise NVMe drives in 2.5-inch form factor using 4-lane PCIe.

prompt: A technician installs a new high-end GPU that requires supplemental power. The GPU has two 8-pin PCIe power connectors. Where must these cables be connected?

options.text: To the SATA power connectors on the motherboard
To the 24-pin ATX main power connector — it handles all GPU power
To the PSU's PCIe power cables (6-pin or 8-pin cables from the power supply)
To the CPU power connector (4-pin or 8-pin EPS connector)

explanation: Power connector types: 24-pin ATX: main motherboard power. Provides 3.3V, 5V, and 12V to the motherboard and slotted expansion cards. Cannot supply enough power for high-end GPUs. 8-pin EPS (CPU): powers the CPU VRM (voltage regulator module). High-end CPUs use 2×8-pin (16-pin total). PCIe power (6-pin = 75W, 8-pin = 150W, 16-pin/12VHPWR = 600W): supplemental power directly to the GPU. High-end GPUs (RTX 4080, RX 7900 XT) require significant supplemental power beyond what the PCIe slot provides (75W max from the slot). SATA power: 15-pin connector for SATA drives — 5V and 12V. NOT appropriate for GPU power. Molex (4-pin): legacy peripheral power — fans, older drives. Some PSUs include adapters (SATA or Molex to PCIe 6/8-pin) but using adapters for high-power GPUs can cause fires — only use native PCIe power cables. The 220-1201 exam tests all major connector types and their purposes.

prompt: A user's external SSD advertises 'USB 3.2 Gen 2×2' speeds. What is the maximum theoretical transfer speed of this connection?

options.text: 5 Gbps — USB 3.2 Gen 1 (formerly USB 3.0)
10 Gbps — USB 3.2 Gen 2 (formerly USB 3.1 Gen 2)
20 Gbps — USB 3.2 Gen 2×2 uses two 10 Gbps lanes simultaneously
40 Gbps — Thunderbolt 4 speed

explanation: USB speed standards (confusing naming history): USB 2.0: 480 Mbps (High Speed). USB 3.2 Gen 1 (formerly USB 3.0, USB 3.1 Gen 1): 5 Gbps (SuperSpeed). USB 3.2 Gen 2 (formerly USB 3.1 Gen 2): 10 Gbps (SuperSpeed+). USB 3.2 Gen 2×2: 20 Gbps — uses two lanes of 10 Gbps simultaneously. Requires USB-C connector. USB4 Gen 2×2: 20 Gbps. USB4 Gen 3×2: 40 Gbps (same as Thunderbolt 3/4). Thunderbolt 3: 40 Gbps. Thunderbolt 4: 40 Gbps (stricter minimum requirements for video and USB4 compatibility). Thunderbolt 5: 80/120 Gbps. Key connector note: USB 3.2 Gen 2×2 and USB4 require USB-C connectors — they cannot use USB-A physically due to the multi-lane requirement. For practical transfer speed: 20 Gbps theoretical = ~2,500 MB/s real-world (NVMe SSDs can saturate this).

prompt: A laser printer has been printing thousands of pages but recently starts picking up multiple sheets at once and jamming frequently. Which component is MOST likely worn out?

options.text: The fuser assembly — worn heating rollers
The imaging drum — reduced photosensitivity
The pickup and separation rollers — worn rubber no longer grabs single sheets reliably
The transfer corona wire — weakened electrostatic charge

explanation: Laser printer paper feed issues: Pickup roller: a rubber roller that pulls paper from the tray into the paper path. Separation roller/pad: prevents multiple sheets from being picked up together — separates the stack and allows only one sheet at a time. When these rubber components wear out (typically after 50,000-100,000 pages depending on paper type): Multiple sheet pickup (multi-feed): worn separation roller no longer holds back extra sheets. Paper jams: sheets arrive at the wrong time, overlap, or misfeed. Fix: replace the pickup and separation roller maintenance kit (specific to the printer model). Preventive maintenance: most laser printers have scheduled maintenance intervals — replace rollers, fuser, transfer belt at the specified page count. Fuser failure: toner smears when touched (not bonded to paper). Drum failure: faded print, ghosting, or streaks. Corona wire failure: completely blank or very faint pages.

prompt: A retail store's receipt printer produces blank receipts even after replacing the paper roll. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The ink cartridge is empty — replace it
The paper is loaded backwards — thermal paper is heat-sensitive on only one side
The printer needs a new ribbon — thermal transfer printers use ink ribbons
The USB connection is faulty — the printer is not receiving print data

explanation: Direct thermal printers use heat-sensitive paper with a thermal coating on one side — the printhead heats specific areas to create black marks. No ink, toner, or ribbon required. Common failure cause: blank output = paper is loaded upside down (coated side facing away from the printhead). Identify the coated side: scratch the paper with a fingernail — the coated side scratches dark. Or hold paper near a heat source — the correct side darkens first. Thermal transfer printers: use a ribbon (wax, resin, or wax-resin) with heat to transfer ink to paper — used for labels and barcodes that must last years without fading. These DO use ribbons. Direct thermal receipts fade over time with heat, UV light, and friction — not suitable for long-term archiving. Receipt/ATM/point-of-sale printers, shipping label printers, and older fax machines use direct thermal. Thermal printers require no ink/toner maintenance — just replace the paper roll.

prompt: A graphic designer needs a monitor with the best possible color accuracy for print work. Which monitor specification is MOST important for this use case?

options.text: Highest refresh rate (240Hz) — more frames per second
Lowest response time (1ms) — fastest pixel transition
Highest color gamut coverage (100% sRGB, AdobeRGB, or DCI-P3)
Highest resolution possible regardless of panel type

explanation: Monitor specs for different use cases: Color gamut: the range of colors a monitor can reproduce. sRGB: standard for web/digital media. AdobeRGB: wider gamut, important for print work (covers more colors printing can reproduce). DCI-P3: cinema/video standard. For print work: high AdobeRGB coverage (90%+ ideal, 100% for professional work) ensures colors on screen match printed output. IPS panels: best color accuracy and wide viewing angles — standard for color-critical work. OLED: perfect blacks and excellent color, but burn-in risk for static content. Refresh rate (Hz): important for gaming (144-360Hz), irrelevant for print work. Response time (ms): important for gaming (reduces motion blur), irrelevant for static design work. Resolution: higher is better for detail work, but panel color accuracy matters more than pixel count for color-critical applications. Hardware calibration: professional designers use a colorimeter (X-Rite, Datacolor) to calibrate monitors to a specific color temperature and gamma — ensures accurate color regardless of ambient light.

prompt: A video editor compares two CPUs: CPU A has 8 cores at 3.8 GHz, and CPU B has 16 cores at 3.2 GHz. For video rendering (which benefits from parallelism), which CPU will MOST likely perform better?

options.text: CPU A — higher clock speed always means better performance
CPU B — more cores allow more video frames to be processed simultaneously, outweighing the lower clock speed for parallelized workloads
Both perform identically — core count and clock speed cancel each other out
CPU A — single-core performance is the only metric that matters for all tasks

explanation: CPU performance factors: Clock speed (GHz): how many instruction cycles per second per core. Higher is better for single-threaded tasks (games, some older applications). Core count: how many independent processing units. More cores allow more tasks to run simultaneously (parallelism). Video rendering is highly parallelizable: each frame or segment of a video can be rendered on a separate core. Software like Adobe Premiere, DaVinci Resolve, and Handbrake scales well across many cores. For rendering: more cores generally wins over higher clock speed. For gaming: higher single-core clock speed matters more (games often can't utilize more than 8-12 cores effectively). Threads (SMT/Hyperthreading): each core can handle 2 threads — 16-core CPU = 32 threads. Cache: L3 cache reduces main memory access latency. TDP (Thermal Design Power): indicates cooling requirements. The 220-1201 asks about basic CPU specs — know cores, threads, clock speed, and their practical implications.

prompt: A technician needs to change the boot order so the PC boots from a USB drive first. Where is this setting configured?

options.text: Device Manager — manages boot device drivers
Disk Management — assigns drive letters and partitions
BIOS/UEFI setup utility — accessed by pressing a key (Del, F2, F10, F12) during POST
Windows Recovery Environment — only accessible after Windows starts

explanation: BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) or UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) is firmware stored on the motherboard that: Initializes hardware during POST. Provides the boot manager (which device to boot from and in what order). Allows configuration of hardware settings (XMP/EXPO memory profiles, Secure Boot, virtualization/VT-x, fan curves, overclocking). Access: press a key during POST (before Windows loads). Common keys: Del or F2 (most motherboards), F10 (HP), F1 (Lenovo ThinkPad), F12 (some systems for boot menu only). UEFI advantages over legacy BIOS: Supports drives over 2TB (GPT), faster boot (UEFI POST), Secure Boot (prevents unauthorized bootloaders), graphical mouse-enabled interface, network flashing. Boot order configuration: BIOS → Boot menu → move USB above HDD/SSD. Or use one-time boot menu (F12 on many systems) to boot from USB without permanently changing boot order.

prompt: A user plugs a Thunderbolt 3 device into their laptop's Thunderbolt 4 port. What should happen?

options.text: Nothing — Thunderbolt 4 and Thunderbolt 3 are incompatible
The device works but at USB 3.2 speeds only — Thunderbolt downsamples
The Thunderbolt 3 device works normally — Thunderbolt 4 is backward compatible with Thunderbolt 3
The laptop requires a firmware update to support older Thunderbolt versions

explanation: Thunderbolt backward compatibility: Thunderbolt 4 is fully backward compatible with Thunderbolt 3 (same 40 Gbps max bandwidth, same USB-C connector). Thunderbolt 3 devices work in Thunderbolt 4 ports at Thunderbolt 3 speeds. Thunderbolt 4 requirements are stricter than Thunderbolt 3: minimum 40 Gbps to two 4K displays (TBT3 only required to one 4K), PCIe 32 Gbps (TBT3 had minimum 16 Gbps), Intel VT-d DMA protection required. USB-C port hierarchy (what fits in what): All Thunderbolt 3/4 ports are USB-C, but NOT all USB-C ports support Thunderbolt. A Thunderbolt cable can carry USB4/USB3/USB2 signals. A USB-C cable may not support Thunderbolt speeds (check the cable rating). Thunderbolt cable identification: Thunderbolt logo (⚡) on the connector or port. Thunderbolt 5 (2023): 80 Gbps bidirectional, 120 Gbps burst (video output direction).

prompt: A color laser printer produces output where all cyan elements are missing and the page looks orange-tinted. Which consumable needs to be replaced?

options.text: The fuser assembly — it controls all color output
The cyan toner cartridge or imaging drum — the cyan color path has failed
The yellow toner cartridge — yellow and cyan create green, so both are affected
The transfer belt — it handles all color output simultaneously

explanation: Color laser printers use four toner colors: Cyan, Magenta, Yellow, Black (CMYK). Each color has its own toner cartridge and typically its own imaging drum (in some designs). When cyan is missing: pages appear with a warm/orange tint because cyan's complementary effect is removed. Blues become purple (no cyan + magenta), greens disappear (no cyan + yellow). Troubleshooting: Remove and reinstall the cyan cartridge — check if it's empty or the contacts are dirty. Shake the cartridge gently if low. Replace if empty. If a new cartridge doesn't fix it, the cyan imaging drum or developer unit may have failed. Color laser printer CMYK process: each color is applied in separate passes on the transfer belt (or drum-to-paper directly in some designs), then all four colors are fused simultaneously. Transfer belt failure: typically affects all colors or creates registration errors (misaligned color layers). The fuser fuses all colors at once — a fuser failure affects all colors, not just one.

prompt: A developer runs a virtual machine on their laptop and wants the VM to be accessible from other computers on the same office network — as if it were a separate physical machine with its own IP address. Which VM network mode should be configured?

options.text: NAT (Network Address Translation) — the VM shares the host's IP address
Host-Only — the VM can only communicate with the host laptop
Bridged — the VM connects directly to the physical network and gets its own IP address
Internal Network — VMs can communicate with each other but not the host or external network

explanation: Virtual machine network modes (VMware/VirtualBox): Bridged: the VM's virtual NIC is bridged directly to the host's physical NIC. The VM appears as a separate physical device on the network. Gets its own IP from the network's DHCP server (or static configuration). Other devices on the network see and can connect to the VM. Use case: servers in VMs that need to be accessed from the network. NAT: the host acts as a router — the VM gets a private IP (typically 192.168.x.x on a VMware-internal subnet). The VM can access the internet through the host but external devices cannot initiate connections to the VM. Use case: development/testing where the VM needs internet but doesn't need to be reached externally. Host-Only: a private network between host and VM only. No internet access for the VM. Use case: isolated testing environments. Internal: VMs can communicate with each other only — no host access, no internet. Use case: simulating isolated network segments.

prompt: A company wants to run 5 virtual machines simultaneously on a single server. Each VM is configured with 4 vCPUs and 8 GB RAM. What is the MINIMUM physical RAM the server needs to run all VMs simultaneously?

options.text: 8 GB — VMs share memory dynamically
40 GB — 5 VMs × 8 GB each, plus overhead for the hypervisor
160 GB — multiply vCPUs by RAM for each VM
Any amount — VMs use virtual memory from disk automatically

explanation: VM resource planning: RAM: each VM is allocated dedicated RAM. 5 VMs × 8 GB = 40 GB minimum for the VMs themselves. The hypervisor (VMware ESXi, Hyper-V, Proxmox) needs additional RAM for itself (typically 4-8 GB for ESXi). Practical minimum: 40 GB VM RAM + 8 GB hypervisor = 48 GB. Recommend 64 GB for headroom. vCPU overcommit: unlike RAM, vCPUs CAN be overcommitted — more vCPUs assigned than physical CPU cores. Modern hypervisors schedule vCPU time on physical cores. 5 VMs × 4 vCPUs = 20 vCPUs — a server with 16 physical cores can still run this with some performance impact. RAM overcommit: some hypervisors support memory ballooning and transparent page sharing to reduce physical RAM needs, but this impacts performance. Best practice: don't overcommit RAM in production. Storage: each VM needs disk space for its virtual disk files (VMDK, VHD/VHDX). Network: physical NICs can be shared among VMs using virtual switches.

prompt: A call center deploys thin client terminals at every desk. Each agent's Windows desktop actually runs on a central server and is streamed to the terminal. What technology is this?

options.text: Application virtualization — only specific apps run virtualized
VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure) — complete desktop environments hosted on servers and delivered to thin clients
Cloud bursting — desktop workloads move to the cloud during peaks
Type 2 hypervisor — the desktop runs on a virtual machine on the thin client

explanation: VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure): full Windows (or Linux) desktop environments run as VMs on a central server farm. Users connect from thin clients, zero clients, or any endpoint via RDP, ICA, or PCoIP protocols. Administrators manage all desktops from a central management console. Benefits: centralized updates (patch once, applies to all VMs), data stays in the data center (better security), thin clients are cheap and durable, easy to provision new desktops. Challenges: network dependency (no local processing), high server infrastructure cost, latency-sensitive for graphics-intensive work. Key products: VMware Horizon, Citrix Virtual Apps and Desktops, Microsoft Azure Virtual Desktop. Application virtualization (App-V, Citrix): only specific applications run in a virtualized container — they can be streamed to standard PCs without full VDI infrastructure. Thin client: a device with minimal local processing, relies on a server for computing. Zero client: no local OS at all — pure remote display protocol device.

prompt: A security analyst receives a suspicious email attachment. Before opening it on a real system, they open it in an isolated environment that monitors its behavior and prevents any damage to the host system. What is this environment called?

options.text: A virtual machine snapshot
A sandbox — an isolated execution environment that observes software behavior safely
A honeypot — a decoy system designed to attract attackers
A DMZ — a network zone between the internet and internal network

explanation: A sandbox is a controlled, isolated environment that allows untrusted software to run while being monitored, preventing it from making persistent changes to the real system or accessing real data. Uses in IT: Malware analysis: run suspicious files in a sandbox and observe their behavior (network connections, file creation, registry changes, process injection). Browser isolation: websites run in a sandboxed browser tab or a full cloud browser (Menlo Security, Zscaler) — even if a site exploits a browser vulnerability, the sandbox prevents access to the host. App sandboxing (iOS/Android): each app runs in its own sandbox and cannot access other apps' data. Windows Sandbox: built-in Windows 11 Pro feature — a lightweight VM running a clean Windows environment that resets to clean state on every restart. Cloud-based sandbox analysis: Hybrid Analysis, AnyRun, Cuckoo Sandbox, Cisco Threat Grid. Honeypot: a decoy system designed to attract real attackers for study — the analyst doesn't control what attacks come in. VM snapshot: saves VM state for rollback — not the same as an analysis sandbox.

prompt: A storage administrator creates a virtual disk for a new VM. The VM is allocated 500 GB, but only 20 GB of data is currently stored. With thin provisioning, how much physical storage is actually consumed immediately?

options.text: 500 GB — the full allocation is reserved on the datastore
250 GB — thin provisioning uses 50% of allocated space
Approximately 20 GB — thin provisioning only uses physical space for actual data written
0 GB — thin provisioned disks use no space until the VM is powered on

explanation: Thick vs Thin VM disk provisioning: Thin provisioning: the virtual disk file starts small and grows as data is written to it. A 500 GB thin disk with 20 GB of data = ~20 GB on the datastore. Advantage: saves physical storage when VMs don't use their full allocation. Risk: if many thin disks grow simultaneously, the datastore can run out of space (overcommit risk) — must monitor datastore usage carefully. Thick provisioning (Eager Zeroed): the full 500 GB is pre-allocated AND pre-zeroed on the datastore immediately. Best performance (no disk growth overhead) and no overcommit risk. Used for databases and high-performance VMs. Thick provisioning (Lazy Zeroed): the full 500 GB is reserved immediately (physically allocated) but not pre-zeroed — zeros are written on first write. For the 220-1201: thin = efficient storage use with overcommit risk; thick = full allocation, better performance, no overcommit risk. Most cloud providers use thin provisioning by default.

prompt: Several keys on a laptop keyboard type wrong characters — pressing 'j' types '1', 'm' types '0', and 'l' types '3'. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The keyboard driver is corrupted — reinstall it
Num Lock is enabled — the right side of the keyboard is mapped to a numeric keypad overlay
The keyboard hardware has failed — replace the keyboard
A virus is remapping keyboard inputs — run a malware scan

explanation: This is a classic Num Lock issue on laptop keyboards. Many laptops lack a dedicated numeric keypad, so keys on the right side of the keyboard double as a numeric keypad when Num Lock is enabled. The affected keys (j→1, k→2, l→3, m→0, u→4, i→5, o→6, etc.) match the embedded numeric keypad overlay. Fix: press the Fn+Num Lock key combination (varies by laptop brand — Fn+F11, Fn+Num Lock, etc.). Check the keyboard for a Num Lock indicator LED. On some laptops, Num Lock activates automatically when connecting an external numeric keypad. If the Fn key is stuck: some laptops have an FnLock mode (press Fn+Esc or Fn+F6 on some brands) that swaps the Fn key behavior. Similar issue: pressing Fn+F7 or similar accidentally enables/disables the touchpad — recognizing Fn lock states is important for laptop troubleshooting.

prompt: A laptop's screen appears very dim even at maximum brightness setting. Shining a flashlight on the screen reveals a faint image. What has most likely failed?

options.text: The GPU — it can no longer drive the display at full brightness
The LCD panel — the pixels have burned out
The backlight (LED or inverter/CCFL) — the image exists but cannot be illuminated
The display cable — it partially disconnects causing reduced brightness

explanation: The faint image visible with a flashlight is the critical diagnostic clue: the LCD panel is working correctly (producing an image), but the backlight that makes it visible has failed. LCD display system components: LCD panel: liquid crystal cells that control light passage to create the image. Backlight: illuminates the panel from behind so the image is visible. Modern laptops use LED backlights. Older laptops used CCFL (Cold Cathode Fluorescent Lamp) backlights powered by an inverter board. Inverter (CCFL only): converts DC power to the AC high voltage needed by CCFL bulbs. If the inverter fails, the CCFL cannot light up. LED backlight failure: the entire LED strip fails, or the driver circuit fails — the screen goes dark but the image remains. Repair options: replace the LED backlight strip, or replace the entire display assembly (screen + cable + bezel). The display cable (LVDS or eDP) failure: typically causes no image at all, flickering, horizontal/vertical lines, or color abnormalities — not just dimness.

prompt: A laptop user reports the cursor jumps randomly while typing and clicks unexpectedly. Which setting should the technician check first?

options.text: Replace the touchpad hardware — random jumps indicate hardware failure
Check if the palm rejection sensitivity is too low or disable touchpad while typing in touchpad settings
Update the touchpad driver — outdated drivers cause cursor jumping
Replace the keyboard — it is sending incorrect signals to the touchpad

explanation: Cursor jumping during typing is almost always caused by accidental palm contact with the touchpad. When typing, the side of the palm or fingers accidentally touch the touchpad, registering as cursor movement or a click. Solutions: Palm rejection setting: most modern touchpad drivers have palm rejection (also called 'disable touchpad when typing'). Adjust sensitivity in Settings → Devices → Touchpad (Windows) or System Preferences → Trackpad (macOS). Disable touchpad while typing: most drivers offer a setting to disable the touchpad for a set duration after keyboard activity. Hardware disabling: press the touchpad enable/disable key (often Fn + F7, F9, or a dedicated touchpad key). External mouse: if the user prefers a mouse, disable the touchpad entirely. If solutions don't help: check if the touchpad driver is current. The physical touchpad may develop faults that cause random input — in that case, driver updates or hardware replacement is needed. But always check settings first before assuming hardware failure.

prompt: A technician needs to replace a failing HDD with a new SSD in a user's laptop while preserving the OS, applications, and all data without reinstalling Windows. What process accomplishes this?

options.text: Copy all files from the HDD to the SSD using File Explorer
Perform a disk clone using imaging software (Macrium Reflect, Clonezilla, or manufacturer tools) to create an exact sector-by-sector copy of the HDD to the SSD
Install Windows on the SSD and use Windows Easy Transfer to migrate data
Use the Windows backup tool to back up and restore to the new SSD

explanation: Disk cloning copies the entire source drive — MBR/GPT, all partitions (boot partition, Windows OS partition, recovery partition), and all data — to the destination drive. The cloned SSD boots identically to the original HDD. Tools: Macrium Reflect Free: excellent for Windows — creates a live clone while the system runs. Clonezilla: free, open-source, bootable USB — highly flexible. Samsung Data Migration: Samsung's free tool for cloning to Samsung SSDs. Acronis True Image: commercial, very user-friendly. Process: connect the SSD (via USB enclosure or second drive bay), run cloning software, clone HDD to SSD, swap drives, boot from SSD. If SSD is smaller than HDD: must first shrink Windows partitions to fit within SSD capacity. File copy (File Explorer): copies only user-visible files — misses system files, boot sector, hidden partitions. Windows Easy Transfer: migrates user data and settings, not a full OS clone. Windows Backup: creates a backup image but requires more steps to restore to new hardware.

prompt: A technician follows this diagnostic sequence: (1) ping 127.0.0.1 — success. (2) ping 192.168.1.1 (default gateway) — fails. (3) Check ipconfig — shows APIPA address 169.254.x.x. What is the correct conclusion?

options.text: The internet service provider is down
DNS is not resolving — the gateway is unreachable because of name resolution failure
DHCP has failed — the device cannot reach the DHCP server and has self-assigned an APIPA address; check physical connection, DHCP server, and network path
The network adapter driver is corrupted — reinstall it

explanation: This diagnostic sequence tells a clear story: Step 1 — ping 127.0.0.1 (loopback) succeeds: the local TCP/IP stack is functioning. The network adapter and drivers are working. Step 2 — ping 192.168.1.1 (gateway) fails: cannot reach the default gateway. Could be physical, DHCP, or routing issue. Step 3 — APIPA address (169.254.x.x): the device tried to get an IP from DHCP but failed, so Windows auto-assigned an APIPA address. An APIPA address cannot communicate beyond the local link — that is why the gateway ping fails. Root cause: DHCP failure. Possible causes: cable unplugged or switch port down (check link lights), DHCP server is down or out of leases, DHCP relay missing on a remote subnet, wrong VLAN on the switch port, Windows DHCP client service stopped. Fix sequence: check physical connection, try ipconfig /release && /renew, verify DHCP server is running, check switch port configuration.

prompt: CrystalDiskInfo shows a hard drive with 47 'Reallocated Sectors Count' and 12 'Current Pending Sectors.' The drive is currently accessible. What should the technician do?

options.text: The drive is fine — these values are within acceptable tolerances
Immediately back up all data and replace the drive — reallocated and pending sectors indicate physical drive degradation and imminent failure
Run chkdsk /f to fix the sectors and continue using the drive
Update the hard drive firmware to fix the bad sectors

explanation: SMART (Self-Monitoring Analysis and Reporting Technology) attributes: Reallocated Sectors Count: when the drive detects a bad sector during write, it marks it bad and replaces it with a spare sector (remapping). Any non-zero value is a serious warning — the drive is physically failing. The spare sector pool is finite; when exhausted, data loss begins. Current Pending Sectors: sectors the drive suspects are bad during reads but hasn't yet attempted to remap. Data in these sectors may be unreadable. Uncorrectable Sector Count: sectors that failed during remapping — data in these sectors is permanently lost. Any of these SMART warnings = imminent drive failure. Response: immediately back up ALL data (the drive may fail completely at any moment). Replace the drive with a new one. Do NOT rely on chkdsk to fix hardware-level sector failures — chkdsk marks bad sectors in the file system but cannot fix physical media damage. Firmware updates cannot repair physical media degradation. SMART monitoring tools: CrystalDiskInfo (Windows), smartmontools (Linux/macOS), HDAT2 (bootable).

prompt: After a Windows 11 update, a USB-connected laser printer no longer works. The printer shows 'offline' in Windows. All cables are connected. What should the technician try first?

options.text: Replace the printer — Windows updates commonly break older hardware permanently
Check if the printer is set to 'Use Printer Offline' in the Windows print queue, and update or reinstall the printer driver
Roll back the Windows update — it is always the cause of printer issues
Move the printer to a different USB port and reformat the hard drive

explanation: Post-Windows-Update printer issues are common. Troubleshooting steps: Check 'Use Printer Offline' mode: open Devices and Printers → right-click the printer → See what's printing → Printer menu → if 'Use Printer Offline' is checked, uncheck it. This is a common accidental setting. Update the driver: Windows Update sometimes replaces OEM drivers with generic drivers. Go to the printer manufacturer's website and download the latest Windows 11-compatible driver. Uninstall and reinstall: Devices and Printers → right-click → Remove device → reinstall the driver. Restart the Print Spooler service (services.msc). Run the printer troubleshooter: Settings → System → Troubleshoot → Other troubleshooters → Printer. Check for a new firmware update for the printer itself. Rolling back Windows updates as a first step is disruptive and rarely necessary — driver updates should be tried first. Never reformat for a printer issue.

prompt: After making changes in UEFI/BIOS, a PC no longer posts and shows a black screen. The technician cannot get back into BIOS setup. What is the MOST likely fix?

options.text: Replace the CPU — it was damaged by the wrong BIOS settings
Clear the CMOS using the motherboard jumper or by removing the CMOS battery for 30 seconds — this resets all BIOS settings to factory defaults
Re-flash the BIOS from a USB drive through Windows
Replace the motherboard — BIOS corruption is permanent

explanation: CMOS (Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor) stores BIOS/UEFI settings using a small coin cell battery (CR2032) for power retention when the PC is off. If wrong BIOS settings prevent booting (e.g., wrong memory timings, overclock failure, disabled video output, wrong boot device), the CMOS reset restores all settings to factory defaults. Methods to clear CMOS: CLRJMP jumper: most motherboards have a two or three-pin header labeled CLR_CMOS or JBAT1. Move the jumper from pins 1-2 to pins 2-3 for 5-10 seconds (per manual), then back. Or short the two pins with a screwdriver briefly. Remove the CMOS battery: unplug the PC, remove the CR2032 battery from the motherboard for 30 seconds (or 5+ minutes to be certain), then reinstall. Some motherboards have a dedicated CMOS_RESET button on the I/O panel. After CMOS reset: re-enter BIOS, configure correct settings (XMP/EXPO, boot order), save and exit. This is not a permanent fix for actual BIOS corruption — that requires reflashing.

prompt: A PC with an AIO (All-in-One) liquid cooler shows high CPU temperatures (95°C+ at idle) despite the pump running and fans spinning. What should the technician check first?

options.text: Replace the CPU — it is generating excessive heat due to hardware failure
Check that the radiator fans are blowing in the correct direction, that the cooler head is properly seated with fresh thermal paste, and that no air bubble is blocking the pump
Replace the entire AIO unit — liquid coolers cannot be serviced
Increase fan speed to maximum in BIOS to cool down the CPU

explanation: AIO liquid cooler troubleshooting with high temps despite pump/fans running: Pump air bubble: if air gets trapped in the pump head, it cannot circulate coolant effectively — the pump makes noise but moves no liquid. Fix: tilt the case while the system runs to move the bubble away from the pump. Thermal paste: the cooler head may not be seated with proper thermal paste coverage. Remove and reapply (pea-sized amount). Mounting pressure: if the cooler isn't firmly mounted with even pressure, there are air gaps reducing thermal transfer. Radiator fan direction: fans should push or pull air through the radiator — incorrect fan direction pushes hot exhaust back through. Exhaust: radiator should exhaust hot air OUT of the case, not into it. Coolant degradation: over time (3-5 years), AIO coolant degrades and loses efficiency. Contact corrosion: the copper plate on the CPU contact may be oxidized. AIO lifespan: most AIOs last 3-7 years before pump failure or coolant degradation. Signs of pump failure: 95°C+ at idle, hot radiator but cold CPU block.

prompt: A user connects a laptop to an external monitor via HDMI but the monitor shows 'No Signal.' The laptop display works normally. What should the technician try FIRST?

options.text: Replace the HDMI cable — HDMI cables fail frequently
Reinstall the graphics driver in Safe Mode
Press the display toggle key (Fn+F4, Win+P, or equivalent) to detect and enable the external display
Replace the external monitor — it does not support HDMI

explanation: External monitor 'No Signal' troubleshooting sequence: Step 1: Press Win+P (Windows) or Fn+F4/F7/F8 (varies by laptop) to open display mode selection and toggle between: PC screen only, Duplicate (mirrors laptop on monitor), Extend (separate desktop on monitor), Second screen only. Many users forget this step — the OS simply isn't configured to use the external display yet. Step 2: Check physical connections — reseat both ends of the HDMI cable. Check that the monitor is on the correct input (HDMI 1 vs HDMI 2 vs DisplayPort). Step 3: Try a different cable — HDMI cables can fail, especially if bent repeatedly. Step 4: Test the monitor with a different device to verify the monitor itself works. Step 5: Check Device Manager for display adapter errors. Update or reinstall the graphics driver if needed. Step 6: If the laptop has both integrated and discrete GPUs, check if the HDMI port is connected to the correct GPU (integrated on Intel/AMD, or discrete NVIDIA/AMD). Some laptops route HDMI only through the integrated GPU; some only through the discrete.
